They describe support measures for SMEs/start-ups (e.g., priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, tailored training and communication channels) and note that SMEs’ interests should be taken into account when notified bodies set conformity-assessment fees, with efforts to lower compliance/certification costs (including translation costs).

bench:qa:62.answer_text: The exercise of powers to impose administrative fines is subject to appropriate procedural safeguards under Union and national law, including effective judicial remedies and due process. In addition, each Member State must lay down rules on the extent to which administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State.

bench:qa:63.answer_text: Market‑surveillance authorities are the primary national bodies responsible for supervising AI systems under the EU AI Act in most cases. Where an AI system is based on a general‑purpose AI (GPAI) model and both the model and the system are provided by the same provider, supervision is instead carried out at Union level by the AI Office, which has the powers of a market‑surveillance authority for that purpose. For GPAI systems that can be used directly for at least one high‑risk purpose, market‑surveillance authorities should cooperate with the AI Office to evaluate compliance and to inform the Board and other authorities. They can also request assistance from the AI Office when they cannot conclude an investigation into a high‑risk AI system due to lack of access to information about the underlying GPAI model; in such cases, the mutual‑assistance procedure for cross‑border cases under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies mutatis mutandis. More generally, the AI Office can support market‑surveillance authorities on request and support cross‑border market‑surveillance activities, without prejudice to the authorities’ powers, and it may support joint activities subject to the agreement of the authorities concerned.

bench:qa:64.answer_text:
A market‑surveillance authority can act in relation to certificates in particular where it considers a high‑risk AI system’s conformity is not ensured because a certificate was **unduly issued**. In that case, the authority may **require the notified body** to **suspend or withdraw** the certificate **within a reasonable period** set by the authority, to ensure continuing conformity of high‑risk AI systems on the market.

More generally, where the authority evaluates an AI system and finds it **does not comply** with the Regulation’s requirements and obligations, it must require the operator to take corrective actions (including withdrawal/recall of the system) and **inform the relevant notified body accordingly**, which can trigger certificate follow‑up actions.

(Separately, for testing in real‑world conditions, the market‑surveillance authority can suspend or terminate that testing.)

bench:qa:65.answer_text: Under Article 47(3), where a high-risk AI system is also subject to other Union harmonisation legislation that requires an EU declaration of conformity, a single EU declaration of conformity may be drawn up covering all applicable Union law. In that case, the declaration must contain all information required to identify the Union harmonisation legislation to which the declaration relates. The provider must also keep the EU declaration of conformity up to date as appropriate (and, by drawing it up, assumes responsibility for compliance with the Section 2 requirements).

bench:qa:66.answer_text: For a high‑risk AI system, the CE marking indicates that the provider declares the system is in conformity with the EU AI Act’s requirements for high‑risk systems (Chapter III, Section 2). Where other applicable Union harmonisation legislation also requires CE marking, the same CE marking also indicates the system fulfils the requirements of that other Union law. The CE marking is used to show conformity so the system can be placed on the market/put into service and move freely within the internal market.

bench:qa:67.answer_text: Providers of general‑purpose AI models are expected to comply with (i.e., adhere to) the AI Office’s codes of practice once those codes are in place and they have been invited to adhere to them by the AI Office. The AI Office may invite all providers to adhere; for providers whose models do not present systemic risks, adherence may be limited to the Article 53 obligations unless they explicitly opt into the full code. The AI Office can then monitor providers’ adherence to approved codes of practice.

bench:qa:68.answer_text: The purpose of the Commission’s post‑market monitoring plan template is to lay down detailed provisions that standardise the post‑market monitoring plan by specifying a template and the list of elements that must be included in that plan, which forms part of the technical documentation for the post‑market monitoring system.

bench:qa:69.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, there is no general “exemption” from having a quality‑management system (QMS) for providers of high‑risk AI systems. However, where a provider is already subject to QMS obligations under relevant sectoral Union law, the provider may integrate (“include”) the AI Act’s QMS elements into that existing sectoral QMS, rather than creating a separate standalone QMS.

Separately, for public authorities putting high‑risk AI systems into service for their own use, the QMS rules may be adopted and implemented as part of an existing national or regional QMS framework, taking into account the authority’s sector, competences and organisation.

bench:qa:70.answer_text:
If a substantial modification is made to a high‑risk AI system after it has been placed on the market or put into service, the modified system must undergo a **new conformity assessment procedure**. This applies **regardless of whether** the modified system will be further distributed or will continue to be used by the current deployer.

In addition, any distributor, importer, deployer, or other third party that makes such a substantial modification (and the system remains high‑risk) is **considered a “provider”** for the purposes of the Regulation and is therefore subject to the provider obligations.

(Separately, for high‑risk AI systems that continue to learn, changes that were pre‑determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment and documented in the technical documentation do **not** count as a substantial modification.)

bench:qa:71.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, an incident or malfunctioning that directly or indirectly leads to the death of a person (or serious harm to a person’s health) qualifies as a “serious incident”. Providers’ quality management systems must include procedures for reporting serious incidents in accordance with Article 73.

There is a limited exception for certain Annex III high-risk AI systems: where the provider is already subject to Union legislation with equivalent reporting obligations, the AI Act notification of serious incidents is limited to incidents involving infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights (i.e., Article 3(49)(c)), meaning death-related serious incidents are not within that limited-notification carve-out.

Separately, whistleblower protections apply to reporting infringements of the Regulation under Directive (EU) 2019/1937.

bench:qa:72.answer_text: The timeframe for a market‑surveillance authority to object to a notified body’s designation is not specified in the provided passages.

bench:qa:73.answer_text: A provider can rely on the presumption of conformity when it complies with applicable European harmonised standards, and only to the extent those standards cover the relevant obligations. For general-purpose AI model providers (including those with systemic risk), codes of practice may be used to demonstrate compliance only until a harmonised standard is published; once the harmonised standard is published (and assessed as suitable to cover the relevant obligations), compliance with it grants the presumption of conformity.

bench:qa:74.answer_text:
For a high‑risk AI system, the provider’s instructions for use must include at least:

1) Provider details
- The identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative.

2) System characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations, including
- The intended purpose.
- The level of accuracy (including metrics), robustness and cybersecurity against which the system has been tested/validated and can be expected, plus any known/foreseeable circumstances that may affect those levels.
- Any known or foreseeable circumstances (including reasonably foreseeable misuse) that may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights.
- Where applicable, the system’s technical capabilities/characteristics to provide information relevant to explain its output.
- When appropriate, performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons.
- When appropriate, specifications for input data and/or other relevant information about the training/validation/testing datasets, taking into account the intended purpose.
- Where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately.

3) Pre-determined changes
- Any changes to the system and its performance that were pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment.

4) Human oversight
- The human oversight measures, including technical measures to facilitate deployers’ interpretation of outputs.

5) Resources, lifetime, maintenance
- Required computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and necessary maintenance/care measures (including frequency) to ensure proper functioning, including software updates.

6) Logging support (where relevant)
- A description of mechanisms that allow deployers to properly collect, store and interpret logs.

More generally, the instructions are meant to inform deployers of the system’s intended purpose and proper use, and should cover characteristics/capabilities/limitations and relevant human oversight measures to support informed use.

bench:qa:75.answer_text:
In the EU AI Act framework, the AI Office’s role in AI regulatory sandboxes is primarily to support coordination, visibility, and cooperation across the Union.

- Support and guidance: National competent authorities must inform the AI Office when they establish a sandbox and may request the AI Office’s support and guidance. The AI Office also maintains a public, up-to-date list of planned and existing sandboxes to encourage interaction and cross-border cooperation. [eu-ai-act:article-57:paragraph-15]

- Facilitating cooperation and information-sharing: The AI Office is supported (via the Board) in helping national competent authorities establish and develop sandboxes, and in facilitating cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes. [eu-ai-act:article-66:paragraph-1:point-k]

bench:qa:76.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, “downstream providers” (i.e., providers that build on or integrate a general-purpose AI model/system into their own AI system, including where it becomes a high-risk AI system) have, based on the passages provided, the following obligation/right:

- **Right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of the Regulation**: Downstream providers may submit a duly reasoned complaint and must include at least (a) the point of contact of the provider of the general-purpose AI model concerned, (b) a description of the relevant facts, the provisions concerned, and why they consider there is an infringement, and (c) any other relevant information, including information they gathered themselves. 

In addition, where a general-purpose AI system/model is used as (or as a component of) a high-risk AI system, the Act envisages **close cooperation along the value chain** to enable compliance: providers of general-purpose AI systems should closely cooperate with providers of the relevant high-risk AI systems and with competent authorities to enable compliance with the Regulation’s obligations.

(Other specific “high-risk provider” obligations—e.g., risk management, quality management, technical documentation, etc.—are not detailed in the retrieved passages, so they are not listed here.)

bench:qa:78.answer_text: Deployers must inform the provider (so the incident can be reported) without undue delay and, in any event, no later than 15 days after the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident. The reporting timeline is “immediately” once a causal link (or reasonable likelihood of such a link) between the AI system and the serious incident has been established, and the exact period should take account of the severity of the incident.

bench:qa:79.answer_text: Testing of high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions must not last longer than necessary to achieve its objectives and, in any case, not longer than six months. It may be extended once for an additional six months (i.e., up to 12 months total), subject to prior notification to the market surveillance authority with an explanation of the need for the extension.

bench:qa:80.answer_text: Market-surveillance authorities must treat any information or documentation they obtain in line with the confidentiality obligations laid down in Article 78 of the EU AI Act. In other words, information gathered in the course of market-surveillance activities is subject to the Act’s Article 78 confidentiality regime, and authorities must perform their tasks accordingly.

bench:qa:81.answer_text:
If a market‑surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider an AI system presents a risk, it must evaluate the system for compliance with the AI Act’s requirements and obligations, paying particular attention to risks to vulnerable groups. If risks to fundamental rights are identified, it must also inform and fully cooperate with the relevant national public authorities/bodies, and operators must cooperate as necessary.

Following the evaluation:
- If the system is found non‑compliant, the authority must require the relevant operator, without undue delay, to take appropriate corrective actions to bring it into compliance, or to withdraw or recall it, within a period the authority prescribes (and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period under relevant Union harmonisation legislation), and it must inform the relevant notified body.
- If a high‑risk AI system is compliant with the AI Act but still presents a risk to health/safety, fundamental rights, or other public‑interest protection, the authority must require the relevant operator to take all appropriate measures so that, when placed on the market or put into service, it no longer presents that risk, without undue delay, within a period the authority may prescribe.

bench:qa:82.answer_text: Providers’ accessibility-related obligation in the AI Act is that providers of **high-risk AI systems** must **ensure the system complies with applicable accessibility requirements**, specifically **in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882**.

bench:qa:83.answer_text: A provider must draw up an EU declaration of conformity **for each high‑risk AI system** (in accordance with Article 47). It must be drawn up and then kept available to national competent authorities **for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service** (and provided to authorities upon request). The provider must also keep the declaration **up to date as appropriate**. If other Union harmonisation legislation also requires an EU declaration of conformity, the provider must draw up **a single declaration covering all applicable Union law** for that high‑risk AI system.

bench:qa:84.answer_text:
For AI systems used by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies that fall within the scope of the EU AI Act, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) has a supervisory and enforcement role:

- **Competent authority for supervision:** The EDPS acts as the competent authority responsible for supervising those Union entities under the Regulation. 
- **Market surveillance authority:** The EDPS also acts as their market surveillance authority (with an exception for the Court of Justice of the EU when acting in its judicial capacity).
- **Procedural role in infringement proceedings:** Before the EDPS takes decisions in proceedings about a possible infringement, it must give the Union entity concerned an opportunity to be heard, base decisions only on elements the parties could comment on, and closely associate complainants (if any) with the proceedings.

bench:qa:85.answer_text: Providers must (1) establish and document a post‑market monitoring system that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high‑risk AI system, and (2) base that system on a post‑market monitoring plan. The post‑market monitoring plan must be included as part of the technical documentation (Annex IV), i.e., the technical documentation must contain a detailed description of the post‑market performance evaluation system, including the plan. In addition, providers’ quality management system must cover the setting‑up, implementation and maintenance of the post‑market monitoring system. The Commission is to adopt an implementing act (by 2 February 2026) setting a template and the list of elements to be included in the post‑market monitoring plan.

bench:qa:86.answer_text: If the scientific panel makes a duly substantiated request, the provider of a general-purpose AI model may receive a formal request for information issued by the Commission. In that case, the provider must provide the requested documentation or information, to the extent that access to it is necessary and proportionate for the scientific panel to fulfil its tasks (notably those under Article 68(2)).

bench:qa:87.answer_text: For high-risk AI systems that are related to products covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, a provider can only be exempt (derogate) from the AI Act’s conformity-assessment procedure to the extent that the relevant Union harmonisation legislation itself provides derogations from its conformity-assessment requirements. In other words, no additional or separate exemptions are created by the AI Act for those product-related high-risk AI systems; only the sectoral derogations apply.

bench:qa:88.answer_text: The passages provided do not state the date from which the Regulation’s obligations become applicable to high‑risk AI systems listed in Annex III. They only confirm that Annex III systems are considered high‑risk and that, before placing on the market/putting into service (and before use by certain public deployers), registration in the EU database is required, with an exception for systems in point 2 of Annex III.

bench:qa:89.answer_text: The AI Office’s codes of practice for general‑purpose AI (GPAI) models are meant to be a central, practical tool to help providers comply with the EU AI Act’s obligations. They are drawn up and updated to reflect the state of the art and diverse perspectives, and they cover the obligations both for GPAI providers generally and for GPAI models presenting systemic risks. For systemic risks in particular, the codes should help establish an EU‑level risk taxonomy and focus on concrete risk‑assessment and risk‑mitigation measures. Providers can rely on approved codes of practice to demonstrate compliance, and the AI Office may monitor implementation and compliance including adherence to approved codes. The AI Office may invite providers to adhere to these codes (with limited adherence for non‑systemic GPAI providers unless they opt in to the full code).

bench:qa:90.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must put in place cybersecurity measures and address cybersecurity risks as part of ensuring the system’s cyber resilience against unauthorised attempts to alter its use, behaviour, or performance (including AI-specific vulnerabilities such as data poisoning and adversarial attacks). Where the high-risk AI system is also within the scope of the EU’s horizontal cybersecurity rules for products with digital elements, providers can demonstrate compliance with the AI Act’s cybersecurity requirements by meeting the essential cybersecurity requirements under that cybersecurity legislation, and showing that in the EU declaration of conformity (or relevant parts of it).

bench:qa:91.answer_text:
For high-risk AI systems, providers have two core obligations regarding logs vis-à-vis competent authorities:

- **Keep the automatically generated logs (to the extent under their control):** Providers must retain the logs referred to in Article 12(1) for a period appropriate to the system’s intended purpose, **at least six months**, unless Union or national law provides otherwise (notably data protection law). 

- **Provide access to logs upon a reasoned request:** When a competent authority makes a **reasoned request**, providers must give that authority access to the automatically generated logs (Article 12(1)) **to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control**.

In addition, where an **authorised representative** is mandated, it must, upon a reasoned request, provide competent authorities with the information/documentation needed to demonstrate conformity, **including access to those logs**, to the extent under the provider’s control.

bench:qa:92.answer_text: The maximum fine for providers of general‑purpose AI models for non‑compliance with their obligations is not stated in the passages provided, so it cannot be determined from this context.

bench:qa:93.answer_text: A provider of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk must conduct adversarial testing as part of its obligation to perform model evaluation using state-of-the-art standardised protocols and tools, and to document that testing, with the aim of identifying and mitigating systemic risks.

bench:qa:94.answer_text: In the Union safeguard procedure (Article 81), the AI Office has duties that are supported by the scientific panel. In particular, the scientific panel’s role is to “advise and support the AI Office” by supporting it “in carrying out its duties in the context of the Union safeguard procedure.” Separately, where a market surveillance authority cannot conclude an investigation of a high-risk AI system because it cannot access certain information related to a general-purpose AI model, it may submit a reasoned request to the AI Office; in that case, the AI Office enforces access and must provide the authority (without delay and within 30 days) any information it considers relevant to assess non-compliance.

bench:qa:95.answer_text: For law‑enforcement related high‑risk AI systems, the EU AI Act passage provided does not list specific data fields/content that must be entered in the EU database. It states only that providers must register themselves and information about their AI system in the EU database, and that any substantial modification must also be registered; however, for law‑enforcement (as well as migration/asylum/border control) the registration must be done in a secure, non‑public section of the database with access strictly limited to the Commission and the competent market surveillance authorities. In addition, “electronic instructions for use” are not to be provided for certain high‑risk systems in these areas (Annex III points 1, 6 and 7).

bench:qa:96.answer_text: Providers must establish and maintain a quality‑management system (QMS) as part of ensuring compliance for high‑risk AI systems. The QMS should support completing the required conformity assessment, preparing the relevant documentation, and operating a robust post‑market monitoring system. Where a provider is already subject to QMS (or an equivalent function) obligations under relevant sectoral Union law, the provider may integrate the AI Act QMS elements into that existing sectoral QMS. The approved QMS is also subject to surveillance. The QMS documentation should, among other things, include a list of the AI systems covered under the same QMS.

bench:qa:97.answer_text: A market‑surveillance authority can issue a provisional suspension/restriction (i.e., take appropriate provisional measures to prohibit or restrict making the AI system available or putting it into service, or to withdraw/recall it) when, after it has required the relevant operator to take corrective action within a prescribed period (in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period under applicable Union harmonisation law), the operator does not take adequate corrective action within that period. In that case, the authority must take those provisional measures and notify the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay.

bench:qa:98.answer_text: The AI Office’s single information platform is meant to provide easy-to-use information about the AI Act (the Regulation) for all operators across the Union.

bench:qa:99.answer_text: If a serious incident occurs, the provider must report it to the market surveillance authority(ies) of the Member State(s) where the incident occurred.

bench:qa:100.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, a provider can rely on the “free and open‑source” exception (and thus not be subject to certain provider obligations that would otherwise trigger the need for an authorised representative) only where all of the following conditions are met:

1) The model is released under a free and open‑source licence that allows users to access, use, modify and distribute the model. 
2) The model’s parameters (including weights), information on the model architecture, and information on model usage are made publicly available. 
3) The model is not a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk (the exception does not apply in that case).

In addition, the “free and open‑source” treatment is not meant to cover models that are monetised (e.g., sold, monetised via paid support/services/platform services, or via use of personal data beyond what is exclusively needed to improve security/compatibility/interoperability), even if they are hosted on an open repository (hosting on an open repository alone is not monetisation).

bench:qa:101.answer_text: Deployers who are employers must inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers **before** putting into service or using a high‑risk AI system at the workplace that they will be subject to its use. Where applicable, this must be done in accordance with the relevant Union and national rules and procedures on informing workers and their representatives.

bench:qa:102.answer_text: 10 years after the system has been placed on the market (or put into service, for high-risk AI systems).

bench:qa:103.answer_text: Importers must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, any applicable storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise the system’s compliance with the requirements in Section 2.

bench:qa:104.answer_text: If a provider considers or has reason to consider that a high‑risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation, it must immediately take the necessary corrective actions—bringing the system into conformity, or (as appropriate) withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it. The provider must also inform the distributors of the system and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative, and importers.

bench:qa:105.answer_text:
The European Artificial Intelligence Board must establish two standing sub-groups whose role is to serve as platforms for cooperation and exchange:

- A standing sub-group for **market surveillance authorities**, focused on issues related to **market surveillance**; this sub-group should act as the **Administrative Cooperation Group (ADCO)** for the AI Act (within the meaning of Article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020).
- A standing sub-group for **notifying authorities**, focused on issues related to **notified bodies**.

The Board may also set up other standing or temporary sub-groups to examine specific issues, and may invite advisory forum representatives to sub-groups/meetings as observers where appropriate.

bench:qa:106.answer_text: A provider may rely on a code of practice (Art. 56) to demonstrate compliance with the obligations for general‑purpose AI models (Art. 53(1))—and, where applicable, for general‑purpose AI models with systemic risk (Art. 55(1))—only **until a relevant European harmonised standard is published**. Once harmonised standards exist, compliance with them gives a presumption of conformity to the extent they cover the obligations; if the provider does not adhere to an approved code of practice or does not comply with harmonised standards, it must demonstrate compliance by alternative adequate means for assessment by the Commission.

bench:qa:107.answer_text: The purpose is to identify and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level arising from the development, placing on the market, or use of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, and to ensure the AI Office is alerted to possible systemic risks at Union level.

bench:qa:108.answer_text: Providers of general‑purpose AI models must draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for the model’s pre‑training and training (including content protected by copyright). The summary should be generally comprehensive in scope (e.g., listing the main data collections/sets used and giving a narrative explanation of other data sources), while taking due account of protecting trade secrets and confidential business information. The AI Office is expected to provide a simple template for this summary, and codes of practice may specify the adequate level of detail.

bench:qa:109.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must affix the CE marking to indicate that the AI system conforms with the AI Act’s requirements (i.e., the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements) and any other applicable Union harmonisation legislation that provides for CE marking. If the high-risk AI system is also subject to other Union law requiring CE marking, the CE marking must indicate that the system also fulfils the requirements of that other law. The CE marking must be affixed in accordance with Article 48 (it is an infringement if it is not affixed, or if it is affixed in violation of Article 48).

bench:qa:110.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must report relevant information about serious incidents (and possible corrective measures) **without undue delay** to the **AI Office** and, as appropriate, to **national competent authorities**.

bench:qa:111.answer_text: Under the EU AI Act, non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices in Article 5 can be punished with administrative fines of up to EUR 1,500,000.

bench:qa:112.answer_text: The AI Office’s codes of practice are intended to foster the voluntary application—by AI systems other than high-risk AI systems—of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices that enable applying those requirements. They are also meant to be a practical tool supporting the proper application of the Regulation, with the AI Office (and the Board) monitoring and evaluating whether the codes meet their objectives and adequately cover relevant obligations, and publishing an adequacy assessment.

bench:qa:113.answer_text:
For **high-risk AI systems** (other than those specifically covered by Article 111(1)), if they were **placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026**, the Regulation applies to their operators **only if, from 2 August 2026 onward, the system is subject to “significant changes” in its design**.

Separately, **providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities** must in any case take the necessary steps to comply **by 2 August 2030**.

bench:qa:114.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, providers have an obligation to comply with the EU database registration requirements for certain high-risk AI systems (the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1)). In practice, this means:

- Providers must carry out the required registration in the EU database (failure to do so is treated as non-compliance).
- Providers must also register any substantial modification of a high-risk AI system in the EU database.
- Where registration is carried out by the provider itself, the provider must ensure the correctness of the registered information (specifically, the information referred to in point 3 of Section A of Annex VIII).

Separately, the Commission acts as controller of the EU database and must provide technical/administrative support and ensure accessibility compliance, but that is not a provider reporting duty as such.

bench:qa:115.answer_text: Under the EU AI Act, the AI Office has a supporting and coordinating role for AI regulatory sandboxes: it supports national competent authorities in establishing and developing sandboxes and helps facilitate cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes across the Union.

bench:qa:116.answer_text: A provider must notify the AI Office (Commission) **at the latest two weeks after** either (i) the requirements triggering the presumption of “general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk” **are met**, or (ii) it **becomes known** that the model **will meet** those requirements (e.g., because training plans/compute allocation show the FLOPs threshold will be reached before training completes).

bench:qa:117.answer_text: Providers’ post‑market monitoring obligations include having a post‑market monitoring system that is **based on a post‑market monitoring plan**. That plan must be **included in the technical documentation (Annex IV)**, as part of the description of the post‑market performance evaluation system. More generally, providers must **establish and document** a post‑market monitoring system **proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks** of the high‑risk AI system, and their quality management system must cover the **set‑up, implementation and maintenance** of that post‑market monitoring system. The Commission is to adopt an implementing act by **2 February 2026** setting a **template** and the **list of elements** to be included in the post‑market monitoring plan.

bench:qa:118.answer_text: Providers must grant the market‑surveillance authority access to the source code of a high‑risk AI system, but only upon a reasoned request and only if both conditions are met: (1) access is necessary to assess conformity with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements; and (2) testing/auditing and verifications based on the data and documentation the provider supplied have been exhausted or have proved insufficient.

bench:qa:119.answer_text: The scientific panel’s alerts are meant to support the AI Office’s monitoring of general-purpose AI models by flagging cases that warrant follow-up action. In particular, the panel may issue “qualified alerts” when it has reason to suspect that a general-purpose AI model poses a concrete and identifiable risk at Union level or may meet the criteria for classification as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk—thereby triggering follow-ups such as investigations and ensuring the AI Office is made aware of models that may need systemic-risk classification.

bench:qa:120.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems that are safety components of, or are themselves, products covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (Section A), a provider can only be exempt from (or otherwise derogate from) the AI Act conformity‑assessment procedure to the extent that the applicable Union harmonisation legislation itself provides a derogation from conformity assessment. In other words, no additional or separate exemptions are created by the AI Act for those product‑related high‑risk AI systems; only the derogations already available under the relevant sectoral product legislation apply.

bench:qa:121.answer_text: Providers of general‑purpose AI (GPAI) models must draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for the model’s pre‑training and training (including content protected by copyright). The summary should be generally comprehensive in scope rather than technically detailed, so that parties with legitimate interests (e.g., copyright holders) can exercise and enforce their rights. It should, for example, list the main data collections/sets used (such as major public/private databases or archives) and include a narrative explanation of other data sources. In doing so, providers should take due account of the need to protect trade secrets and confidential business information. The AI Office is expected to provide a simple template for this summary, and it will monitor whether the provider has fulfilled the obligation without conducting a work‑by‑work copyright assessment of the training data.

bench:qa:122.answer_text: The AI Act does not specify a fixed maximum duration (e.g., a number of months) for which a sandbox plan may be in effect. It only requires that activities in an AI regulatory sandbox take place “for a limited time” under a sandbox plan whose “timeframe” is agreed between the provider and the competent authority.

bench:qa:123.answer_text: If a high‑risk AI system continues to learn after being placed on the market/put into service, the provider must ensure it undergoes a new conformity assessment only if there is a **substantial modification**. However, **pre‑determined** changes to the system and its performance (set by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment and included in the technical documentation) **do not count as a substantial modification**, so they do **not** trigger a new conformity assessment.

bench:qa:124.answer_text: A provider of a high‑risk AI system must keep the automatically generated logs referred to in Article 12(1) (to the extent the logs are under the provider’s control) for a period appropriate to the system’s intended purpose, and in any event for at least six months—unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (notably data‑protection law).

bench:qa:125.answer_text:
For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies that fall within the scope of the EU AI Act, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) acts as:

- The competent authority responsible for their supervision.
- Their market surveillance authority (except for the Court of Justice of the EU when acting in its judicial capacity).

In enforcement proceedings, before adopting decisions, the EDPS must give the Union institution/body/office/agency concerned an opportunity to be heard, base decisions only on elements the parties could comment on, and closely associate any complainants with the proceedings.

bench:qa:126.answer_text:
For high-risk AI systems that are only provided digitally, providers should use a **digital CE marking** to indicate conformity with the AI Act’s requirements.

More generally, the CE marking is the marking by which the provider indicates that the AI system conforms with the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 (and any other applicable Union harmonisation legislation requiring CE marking). Where other Union law also requires CE marking, the CE marking must indicate that the high-risk AI system also fulfils the requirements of that other law. Providers must ensure the CE marking is properly affixed (i.e., not missing and not affixed in violation of the CE-marking rules).

bench:qa:127.answer_text: In the event of a serious incident involving the death of a person, the provider must report it to the market‑surveillance authority immediately after it has established—or as soon as it suspects—a causal relationship between the high‑risk AI system and the incident, and in any case no later than 10 days after the provider (or, where applicable, the deployer) becomes aware of the serious incident.

bench:qa:128.answer_text: The purpose of the AI Office/Commission’s guidelines is to provide practical guidance for implementing the Regulation—clarifying how key requirements and obligations should be applied (including Articles 8–15 and 25), how prohibited practices (Article 5) and rules on substantial modification should be handled, how to comply with transparency obligations (Article 50), how the Regulation relates to other EU harmonisation legislation and relevant Union law, and how to apply the definition of an AI system. In doing so, the guidelines should reflect the state of the art and relevant standards/specifications, and pay particular attention to the needs of SMEs (including start-ups), local public authorities, and the sectors most affected.

bench:qa:129.answer_text:
The passages provided do not set out a specific “without prior notice” power or the conditions for suspending a high‑risk AI system without notice.

They describe that, where a market‑surveillance authority identifies non‑compliance during its evaluation, it must “without undue delay” require the relevant operator/provider to take corrective actions, withdraw, or recall the system within a prescribed period (generally within 15 working days), and that Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies to those measures. However, the exact circumstances (if any) in which suspension can occur without prior notice are not stated in the cited text and would depend on the applicable provisions (including Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 Article 18, which is referenced but not reproduced here).

bench:qa:130.answer_text:
Providers of high-risk AI systems must:

- Establish and document a post-market monitoring system, in a way that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system. 
- Base that system on a post-market monitoring plan.
- Include the post-market monitoring plan as part of the technical documentation (Annex IV).
- Ensure their quality management system covers the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of the post-market monitoring system.

In addition, the Commission is to adopt an implementing act (by 2 February 2026) setting a template and the elements to be included in the post-market monitoring plan.

bench:qa:131.answer_text:
The retrieved passages do not state what providers must do specifically when a notified body withdraws a certificate.

They do indicate related obligations in the conformity-assessment context: if the provider intends to introduce (or becomes aware of) changes to an AI system that could affect compliance or intended purpose, the provider must inform the notified body that issued the certificate; the notified body then assesses the changes and decides whether a new conformity assessment is needed or whether a supplement to the certificate can be issued.

bench:qa:132.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must conduct adversarial testing as part of its obligation to perform model evaluation in accordance with state‑of‑the‑art standardised protocols and tools, and to document that testing, with the aim of identifying and mitigating systemic risks.

bench:qa:133.answer_text: Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request under Article 91 is subject to the fines laid down in Article 101. However, the specific maximum amount is not included in the provided excerpts, so it cannot be determined from the cited text alone.

bench:qa:134.answer_text: Providers must ensure that high‑risk AI systems bear the CE marking as the indication that the system conforms with the AI Act’s requirements (Chapter III, Section 2) and any other applicable Union harmonisation legislation requiring CE marking. For high‑risk AI systems embedded in a product, a physical CE marking should be affixed (and it may be complemented by a digital CE marking). For high‑risk AI systems provided only digitally, a digital CE marking should be used. Where other Union law also provides for CE marking, the CE marking must indicate that the high‑risk AI system also fulfils the requirements of that other law. Failure to affix the CE marking, or affixing it in violation of the applicable rules, is treated as non‑compliance for enforcement purposes.

bench:qa:135.answer_text: A provider must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk‑management system for its high‑risk AI system, and run it as a continuous, iterative process throughout the entire lifecycle of the system (with regular review and updating).

bench:qa:136.answer_text: The AI Office’s single information platform is meant to provide easy-to-use information about the AI Act (the Regulation) for all operators across the Union.

bench:qa:0.answer_text: Based on the provided provisions, the Regulation’s primary purpose is to assess and ensure compliance with its requirements (including by enabling the Commission to request documentation and other necessary information for that compliance assessment).

bench:qa:1.answer_text:
Under the AI Regulation, compliance obligations fall on several actors depending on their role and the type of AI system involved. In the provisions provided, obligations are imposed on:

- Providers (including providers of high-risk AI systems), e.g., to comply with registration obligations and to affix the CE marking for high-risk AI systems. 
- Authorised representatives (where applicable), e.g., to comply with registration obligations.
- Deployers (including deployers of high-risk AI systems), e.g., to assign human oversight and, for certain public-sector deployers, to enter/register required information in the EU database.
- Deployers who are (or act on behalf of) public authorities/agencies/bodies, who must enter specified data into the EU database.

Additionally, the text provided indicates that measures must be taken to comply with obligations in Articles 53 and 54 (which concern general-purpose AI models), implying obligations also arise in that area for the relevant actors addressed by those articles.

bench:qa:2.answer_text: No—where an AI system is placed on the market, put into service, or used (with or without modification) **exclusively** for military, defence or national security purposes, the AI Regulation does **not** apply, regardless of the type of entity using it. It also does not apply where an AI system is not placed on the market or put into service in the Union but its output is used in the Union exclusively for those purposes. In addition, the Regulation does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law and does not affect Member States’ competences concerning national security.

bench:qa:3.answer_text: Under the Regulation, an ‘AI system’ means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers— from the input it receives—how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.

bench:qa:4.answer_text: The Regulation does not provide a standalone definition of the term “risk” in Article 3 in the excerpts provided. However, it clarifies that **“AI systems presenting a risk”** are to be understood as a **“product presenting a risk”** (as defined in Article 3(19) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020), **insofar as** the AI system presents **risks to the health or safety, or to the fundamental rights, of persons**.

bench:qa:5.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, the Act does not give a general definition of “provider” of an AI system. However, it specifies that certain actors are treated as (i.e., “shall be considered”) a provider of a high-risk AI system for the purposes of the Regulation.

In particular, any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party shall be considered a provider of a high-risk AI system where they:
- put their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service;
- make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, such that it remains high-risk; or
- modify the intended purpose of an AI system (including a general-purpose AI system) that was not classified as high-risk, in a way that makes it become high-risk.

Separately, the Act refers to “a provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk” (who must document that assessment), but this does not itself define who a provider is in general.

bench:qa:6.answer_text: In the AI Regulation, a “deployer” is the actor expected to use (i.e., put into use) a high-risk AI system in a specific context. This is reflected by provisions that (i) refer to the deployer’s “first use” of a high-risk AI system and duties during its use, and (ii) require instructions for use to be provided to the deployer.

bench:qa:7.answer_text:
The excerpts you provided define “AI literacy” and mention promoting it, but they do not set a specific, direct obligation on providers and deployers to ensure AI literacy.

- Definition: AI literacy is the skills, knowledge and understanding enabling providers, deployers and affected persons—considering their rights and obligations under the Regulation—to make informed deployment of AI systems and to be aware of AI opportunities, risks and possible harm. 
- The Act also refers to “promoting AI literacy”, particularly for persons dealing with the development, operation and use of AI.

No further concrete “required” measures (e.g., mandatory training programmes, minimum content, or documentation duties specifically labelled as AI literacy) are included in the provided provisions.

bench:qa:8.answer_text: From the provided excerpts, Article 5 is referenced as containing a “list of prohibited practices,” but none of the specific prohibited practices themselves are included in the context. Therefore, I can’t name one prohibited AI practice from Article 5 based only on these sources.

bench:qa:9.answer_text: Yes, but only in narrowly limited circumstances. The Act allows the use of “real-time” remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement only for the objectives referred to in Article 5(1)(h), and only to confirm the identity of a specifically targeted individual. Their use must be subject to necessary and proportionate safeguards (including temporal, geographic and personal limitations) under national law authorising the use, and it must be authorised only after the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27) and registered the system in the EU database (Article 49), with a limited urgency exception allowing use before registration if registration follows without undue delay.

bench:qa:10.answer_text:
From the provided excerpts, Article 6 classification is referenced (but not fully set out). What can be stated from the text you provided is:

- A provider may classify an AI system as “non-high-risk” under Article 6(3); if a market surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider that such a system is in fact high-risk, it must evaluate the system’s classification as high-risk based on the conditions in Article 6(3) and Commission guidelines. 
- If a provider considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk, it must document its assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service.
- An AI system can become high-risk “in accordance with Article 6” where a third party modifies the intended purpose of a previously non-high-risk system (including a GPAI system) so that it becomes high-risk.

The specific criteria/conditions in Article 6(1)–(3) for when an AI system is classified as high-risk are not included in the provided context, so I cannot restate them verbatim from these excerpts.

bench:qa:11.answer_text:
Yes, but only under the derogation in Article 6(3): an Annex III system may be treated as non-high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights (including by not materially influencing decision-making) and one of the listed conditions (narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting patterns/deviations without replacing or influencing prior human assessment without proper human review, or a preparatory task) is met. However, an Annex III system must always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons.

If the provider classifies an Annex III system as non-high-risk, it must document its assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service and provide that documentation to competent authorities upon request. A market surveillance authority may evaluate whether a system classified by the provider as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) is in fact high-risk.

bench:qa:12.answer_text: According to Article 8(1), high‑risk AI systems shall comply with the requirements laid down in this Section, taking into account their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI‑related technologies.

bench:qa:13.answer_text:
For high‑risk AI systems, the Act describes the risk management system as a continuous, iterative process across the entire lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating. It must be established, implemented, documented and maintained, and it comprises these main steps:

1) Identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when used as intended.
2) Estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge when used as intended and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse.
3) Evaluate other risks that may arise based on data gathered from the post‑market monitoring system.
4) Adopt appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified.

In addition, high‑risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures, and testing must ensure consistent performance for the intended purpose and compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

Where providers are already subject to internal risk management processes under other Union law, the aspects of Article 9(1)–(9) may be part of, or combined with, those procedures.

bench:qa:14.answer_text: Under Article 10, high‑risk AI systems that use training techniques must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet the Article 10(2)–(5) quality criteria. In particular, the training/validation/testing data sets must be: (1) relevant; (2) sufficiently representative; (3) to the best extent possible, free of errors; (4) complete in view of the intended purpose; and (5) have appropriate statistical properties (including, where applicable, regarding the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used). These characteristics can be met by individual data sets or by a combination of data sets.

bench:qa:15.answer_text:
For a high‑risk AI system, the technical documentation must:

- Be drawn up so as to demonstrate that the system complies with the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, and to provide national competent authorities and notified bodies with the necessary information in a clear and comprehensive form to assess compliance.
- Contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV.

(Separately, the Act also requires that the provider draw it up before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, and keep it up to date.)

bench:qa:16.answer_text: Providers must keep the technical documentation at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years after the high‑risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service.

bench:qa:17.answer_text:
Under Article 12, high‑risk AI systems must have logging capabilities that:

- Enable recording of events relevant to: (a) identifying situations that may result in the system presenting a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) or in a substantial modification; (b) facilitating post‑market monitoring (Article 72); and (c) monitoring the operation of certain high‑risk AI systems (those referred to in Article 26(5)).

In addition, for high‑risk AI systems referred to in Annex III, point 1(a), providers must ensure logging capabilities provide, at a minimum:
- the period of each use of the system (start date/time and end date/time);
- the reference database against which input data has been checked;
- the input data for which the search led to a match; and
- the identification of the natural persons involved in verifying the results (as referred to in Article 14(5)).

bench:qa:18.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs (to the extent the logs are under their control) for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, and in any event for at least six months—unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (in particular Union data protection law).

bench:qa:19.answer_text:
For high‑risk AI systems, the Act requires that deployers receive (via the system’s instructions for use) information that enables them to interpret the system’s output and use it appropriately, as part of the system’s characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (where applicable). In addition, the high‑risk AI system must be provided to the deployer in a way that enables the natural persons assigned human oversight to remain aware of the risk of automation bias (automatic over‑reliance on the system’s output), as appropriate and proportionate.

These transparency duties are in addition to (and do not replace) other transparency obligations for deployers that may exist under Union or national law.

bench:qa:20.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems, human oversight is meant to ensure that assigned natural persons can effectively supervise and control the system’s use and outputs. In particular, the system must be provided so that those persons can: understand the system’s capacities and limitations and monitor its operation to detect and address anomalies or unexpected performance; stay aware of and mitigate automation bias; correctly interpret the system’s outputs; decide not to use the system or disregard/override/reverse its output in a given situation; and intervene in operation or safely stop the system (e.g., via a stop button).

bench:qa:21.answer_text: Under Article 20(1), a provider must withdraw or recall a high‑risk AI system when it considers, or has reason to consider, that a high‑risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation; in that case it must immediately, as appropriate, take the necessary corrective actions, including bringing it into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it.

bench:qa:22.answer_text:
When a competent authority makes a reasoned request, providers of high-risk AI systems must:
- Provide the authority with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate the system’s conformity with the Section 2 requirements, in a language easily understood by the authority and in an official EU language indicated by the Member State concerned.
- Also give the requesting authority access to the system’s automatically generated logs (as referred to in Article 12(1)), to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

In addition, the authority’s request for information must state its legal basis and purpose, specify the information required, set a deadline for providing it, and indicate the potential fines for supplying incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information.

bench:qa:23.answer_text:
A provider must appoint an authorised representative (established in the Union, by written mandate) when the provider is established in a third country:

- For high-risk AI systems: prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market.
- For general-purpose AI models: prior to placing the general-purpose AI model on the Union market.

bench:qa:24.answer_text: Before placing a high‑risk AI system on the market, importers shall ensure the system is in conformity with the Regulation by verifying that: (a) the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure (Article 43); (b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV); (c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and instructions for use; and (d) the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1).

bench:qa:26.answer_text:
A distributor is considered a provider of a high‑risk AI system (and becomes subject to the provider obligations under Article 16) if any of these apply:

(a) The distributor puts its name or trademark on a high‑risk AI system that has already been placed on the market or put into service.

(b) The distributor makes a substantial modification to a high‑risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, and the system remains high‑risk (pursuant to Article 6).

(c) The distributor modifies the intended purpose of an AI system (including a general‑purpose AI system) that was not classified as high‑risk and was already placed on the market or put into service, so that it becomes a high‑risk AI system (in accordance with Article 6).

bench:qa:27.answer_text:
Main obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems (based on the provided extracts) include:

- Monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use. (This monitoring obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities.)
- Keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent those logs are under their control, for an appropriate period for the system’s intended purpose and at least six months, unless Union or national law (notably data protection law) provides otherwise.
- For certain deployers (bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of certain Annex III systems), carry out—prior to deployment—an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights that the use of the system may produce (with an exception for systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III).
- For deployers that are public authorities (or Union institutions/bodies/offices/agencies), comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49.
- For certain Annex III high-risk systems that make or support decisions about natural persons, inform the affected natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system (with a specific rule for law-enforcement use).

Note: Article 26 is explicitly referenced as the source of deployer obligations in the Act’s enforcement provisions.

bench:qa:28.answer_text:
Deployers must conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment **prior to deploying** a **high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2)** when they are **(i) bodies governed by public law**, **(ii) private entities providing public services**, or **(iii) deployers of the high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III points 5(b) and 5(c)**. This obligation does **not** apply to **high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in Annex III point 2**.

In addition, the **use of ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces** may be authorised **only if** the law enforcement authority has **completed** a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 (and registered the system in the EU database).

bench:qa:29.answer_text: Under Article 28, the notifying authority is the national authority that carries out the assessment, designation, notification and ongoing monitoring of notified bodies. In that role, it must be able to obtain and review relevant documentation from notified bodies to conduct those activities. It also serves as an information point vis-à-vis the Commission on matters relating to the notification of a notified body and the maintenance of that body’s competence. If a notified body’s designation is restricted, suspended or withdrawn, the notifying authority must ensure the notified body’s files are kept and made available on request to notifying authorities in other Member States and to market surveillance authorities.

bench:qa:31.answer_text:
The provided context does not include the text of Article 31 itself, so the specific requirements for notified bodies under Article 31 cannot be listed from these excerpts.

From the cited provisions, we can only infer the following about Article 31 requirements:
- A notifying authority may notify only conformity assessment bodies that have satisfied the requirements laid down in Article 31. 
- Notified bodies designated under other Union harmonisation legislation must update their designation documentation when relevant changes occur so the authority responsible for notified bodies can monitor and verify continuous compliance with all Article 31 requirements.
- Notified bodies notified under other legal acts may control conformity of high-risk AI systems with Section 2 requirements only if their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) has been assessed in the notification procedure under those legal acts.
- Third-country conformity assessment bodies may be authorised to carry out notified body activities under the Regulation if they meet Article 31 requirements or ensure an equivalent level of compliance.

To answer your question fully, the actual content of Article 31 (and its paragraphs) is needed.

bench:qa:32.answer_text:
A provider can use a European harmonised standard to demonstrate conformity/compliance once the harmonised standard has been published (i.e., its reference is published in the Official Journal of the European Union). When the provider complies with the harmonised standard, it benefits from a presumption of conformity to the extent the standard covers the relevant obligations.

For general-purpose AI model providers (including those with systemic risk), codes of practice may be used to demonstrate compliance only until a harmonised standard is published; after publication, compliance with the harmonised standard grants the presumption of conformity.

For high-risk AI systems, if the provider has not applied (or has only partly applied) the harmonised standard, or if harmonised standards do not exist, the provider must instead follow the Annex VII conformity assessment procedure in the situations listed in Article 43(1), second subparagraph.

bench:qa:33.answer_text:
“Common specifications” are Commission-developed technical specifications that can be used (alongside harmonised standards) to support compliance with the EU AI Act.

They are used mainly as a compliance route for high-risk AI systems (and also for general-purpose AI models): if a system/model conforms to the relevant common specifications (or parts of them), it is presumed to be in conformity with the covered requirements (or to comply with the covered obligations), to the extent those specifications cover them.

In terms of when they come into play: they are relevant where harmonised standards under Article 40 do not exist and common specifications under Article 41 are not available (a condition referenced in the conformity assessment context). When drafting common specifications, the Commission must consult the advisory forum. Guidelines under the Act must also take due account of relevant harmonised standards and common specifications.

bench:qa:34.answer_text: Based on the provided excerpts, Article 42 “presumption of conformity” relates to harmonised standards or common specifications that confer a presumption of conformity (i.e., using those standards/specifications is treated as evidence of conformity).

bench:qa:35.answer_text:
High-risk AI systems listed in Annex III must undergo “the relevant conformity assessment procedure as referred to in Article 43.” Notified bodies verify conformity of high-risk AI systems in accordance with the conformity-assessment procedures set out in Article 43.

The specific procedures themselves (e.g., which modules/routes apply to which Annex III systems) are not provided in the excerpts you supplied; they are contained in Article 43, which is referenced here but not included in the context.

bench:qa:36.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems covered by Annex I, a certificate of conformity is valid for the period indicated on the certificate, but that period must not exceed five years (and any extension is also limited to further periods of up to five years, based on re‑assessment).

bench:qa:37.answer_text:
If a serious incident occurs, providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market must:

- Report the serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State(s) where the incident occurred. The report must be made immediately after the provider has established a causal link (or a reasonable likelihood of such a link) between the AI system and the incident, and in any event no later than 15 days after the provider (or, where applicable, the deployer) becomes aware of the incident; the reporting period must take account of the severity of the incident.

- After reporting, without delay perform the necessary investigations into the incident and the AI system concerned. This must include a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action.

- Cooperate with the competent authorities (and, where relevant, the notified body) during those investigations.

- Not carry out any investigation that alters the AI system in a way that could affect any subsequent evaluation of the causes of the incident, unless the competent authorities have first been informed of that action.

bench:qa:38.answer_text:
From the cited provisions, the EU database referred to in Article 71 serves as a Union-level registration and information repository for AI systems and their actors, which is then used by other obligations and oversight mechanisms under the Act. In particular:

- It is the database in which providers (or authorised representatives) must register themselves and an AI system before placing it on the market or putting it into service in certain cases (e.g., where the provider concludes the system is not high-risk under Article 6(3)).
- It provides information that market surveillance authorities may use to perform checks when monitoring compliance.
- It supports traceability by enabling references such as the URL of an AI system’s database entry.

Separately, Article 71(6) assigns the Commission as controller of the database and requires it to provide support and ensure accessibility, which underpins the database’s operational purpose.

bench:qa:39.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk AI systems have the following post-market monitoring obligations:

- Establish and document a post-market monitoring system, proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system. (This is the core post-market monitoring duty.)
- Ensure the post-market monitoring system is based on a post-market monitoring plan.
- Include that post-market monitoring plan in the technical documentation (Annex IV), and provide a detailed description of the post-market performance-evaluation system in place, including the plan.
- As part of the provider’s quality management system, set up, implement and maintain the post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72.

Note: the Act also foresees that the Commission will adopt an implementing act establishing a template and required elements for the post-market monitoring plan (by 2 February 2026).

bench:qa:40.answer_text: A provider must register a non‑high‑risk AI system **before placing it on the market or putting it into service**, but only in the specific case where the provider has concluded that the system is **not high‑risk under Article 6(3)**. In that case, the provider (or, where applicable, the authorised representative) must register themselves and the system in the EU database (Article 71).

bench:qa:41.answer_text:
For AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, the EU AI Act imposes a transparency duty on providers:

- Providers must ensure the system is designed and developed so that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system.
- Exception: this informing duty does not apply where it is obvious (from the perspective of a reasonably well‑informed, observant and circumspect natural person), taking into account the circumstances and context of use.
- Additional exception: the duty also does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (subject to appropriate safeguards for third parties’ rights and freedoms), unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence.

These obligations are without prejudice to other transparency obligations in Union or national law that may apply to deployers.

bench:qa:42.answer_text: Under Article 50(4), deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This disclosure obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute a criminal offence. If the deep-fake content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the transparency duty is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated/manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.

bench:qa:43.answer_text: The provided context does not include Article 63 or any definition text for “general‑purpose AI model”. Therefore, I can’t state what Article 63 says it means based on these excerpts.

bench:qa:44.answer_text:
Under Article 51(1), a general‑purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk (“general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk”) if it meets either of these conditions:

1) It has **high‑impact capabilities**, as evaluated using appropriate technical tools and methodologies (including indicators and benchmarks); or

2) The **Commission decides** (on its own initiative or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel) that the model has **capabilities or an impact equivalent** to the high‑impact capabilities in (1), taking into account the criteria in **Annex XIII**.

Exception: even if the model meets condition (1)(a), the provider may submit substantiated arguments showing that, exceptionally, due to its specific characteristics, it does not present systemic risks and therefore should not be classified as systemic‑risk.

bench:qa:45.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk has a notification-related obligation in that, when notifying under Article 51(1)(a), it may include (with its notification) sufficiently substantiated arguments that—exceptionally—although the model meets the relevant threshold, it does not present systemic risks due to its specific characteristics and therefore should not be classified as a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk.

bench:qa:46.answer_text:
From the provisions provided in your context, the obligations (and related compliance routes) for providers of general‑purpose AI (GPAI) models are:

- Demonstrate compliance with the obligations applicable to GPAI model providers (as referenced in Article 53(1)) either by:
  - relying on approved codes of practice (Article 56) to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published; or
  - complying with European harmonised standards (which gives a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the obligations); or
  - if they do not adhere to an approved code of practice and do not comply with a harmonised standard, demonstrating “alternative adequate means of compliance” for assessment by the Commission. 

- Note on codes of practice participation: the AI Office may invite all GPAI model providers to adhere to codes of practice; for providers whose GPAI models do not present systemic risks, adherence may be limited to the obligations in Article 53 (unless they explicitly declare interest to join the full code).

Your excerpt does not include the substantive list of obligations in Article 53(1) itself, so I cannot enumerate those specific duties from the provided text.

bench:qa:47.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not contain the operative rule that sets out *when* an authorised representative is required for providers of general‑purpose AI models (that rule would normally be in Article 22 on authorised representatives, which is only referenced here but not included). From the excerpts available, we can only infer that the Act contemplates “authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union” and that authorised representatives have obligations “pursuant to Article 22,” but the triggering conditions (including any specific application to general‑purpose AI models) are not stated in the supplied text.

bench:qa:48.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, providers of general‑purpose AI (GPAI) models with systemic risk have additional obligations (on top of those in Articles 53 and 54). They must:

- Perform model evaluation using state‑of‑the‑art standardised protocols and tools, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks.
- Assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level (including their sources) that may arise from the development, placing on the market, or use of the systemic‑risk GPAI model.
- Track, document, and report without undue delay to the AI Office (and, as appropriate, national competent authorities) relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures.
- Ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the systemic‑risk GPAI model and its physical infrastructure.

They may use approved codes of practice to demonstrate compliance with these obligations until a harmonised standard is published; compliance with European harmonised standards gives a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the obligations. If they neither adhere to an approved code of practice nor comply with a harmonised standard, they must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission.

bench:qa:49.answer_text: Under the AI Act, references to the “AI Office” are to be understood as references to the European Commission.
