The AI Office’s roles reflected in the provided provisions include: (1) encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of Union-level codes of practice to support effective implementation of obligations on detecting and labelling artificially generated or manipulated content; (2) encouraging and facilitating the review and adaptation of codes of practice (notably in light of emerging standards) and assisting in the assessment of available standards; (3) developing a questionnaire template (including via an automated tool) to help deployers comply with their obligations in a simplified manner; and (4) developing and recommending voluntary model contract terms for high-risk AI supply-chain arrangements, taking into account sector- or use-case-specific contractual requirements.

bench:qa:50.answer_text: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (the “Board”) is a body established by the AI Act. The Act also provides that the Commission must consult the Board when issuing certain guidance, such as guidelines on the practical implementation of Article 6 (high-risk AI systems).

bench:qa:51.answer_text: The advisory forum is established to provide technical expertise and advise the AI Board and the Commission, and to contribute to their tasks under the Regulation. It may also prepare opinions, recommendations and written contributions at the request of the Board or the Commission, and it must prepare an annual report on its activities (made publicly available).

bench:qa:52.answer_text: Under the EU AI Act, the scientific panel of independent experts is intended to support enforcement activities under the Regulation. In particular, the Commission establishes it for that purpose, and Member States may call upon its experts to support their own enforcement activities.

bench:qa:53.answer_text: Member States must designate or establish at least one notifying authority under Article 28(1). The provision does not set a specific deadline; it applies generally (i.e., each Member State must have at least one such authority responsible for the procedures for assessment, designation and notification of conformity assessment bodies and for their monitoring).

bench:qa:54.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, AI regulatory sandboxes are frameworks set up by competent authorities to let providers or prospective providers participate in a controlled setting that supports developing and bringing AI systems to market while improving legal certainty and compliance.

Key features and aims in the Act include:
- Objectives: improving legal certainty for compliance with the AI Act (and where relevant other law), sharing best practices with participating authorities, fostering innovation and competitiveness, enabling evidence-based regulatory learning, and facilitating/accelerating access to the EU market (especially for SMEs and start-ups). (eu-ai-act:article-57:paragraph-9)
- Access and operation (via implementing acts): sandboxes must be open to any applying provider/prospective provider meeting transparent and fair eligibility/selection criteria; allow broad and equal access; support flexibility for national authorities to establish and operate them; be free of charge for SMEs (subject to limited recovery of exceptional costs); have simple/clear procedures; be mutually and uniformly recognised across the Union with the same legal effects; and participation is time-limited to a period appropriate to the project (extendable). They should also facilitate compliance learning (e.g., conformity assessment) and involve relevant ecosystem actors, and support testing/benchmarking/assessment and risk-mitigation learning. (eu-ai-act:article-58:paragraph-2)
- EU-level support and interface: the Commission must create a single dedicated interface with information on sandboxes so stakeholders can interact with them, raise enquiries, and seek non-binding guidance on conformity of innovative AI-enabled products/services/business models; and the AI Office assists and facilitates cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes. (eu-ai-act:article-57:paragraph-17, eu-ai-act:article-66:paragraph-1:point-k)

bench:qa:55.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not state a specific deadline or date by which AI regulatory sandboxes must be operational. They describe objectives for establishing sandboxes and requirements for implementing acts and design/implementation, but no “by when” obligation is included in the cited provisions.

bench:qa:56.answer_text:
Testing high‑risk AI systems in real‑world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes may be conducted by providers or prospective providers of Annex III high‑risk AI systems only in accordance with Article 60 and a “real‑world testing plan”, and without prejudice to Article 5 prohibitions and any other applicable Union/national testing law (including any ethical review requirements). Key requirements/conditions include:

- A real‑world testing plan must be drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority (MSA) in the Member State where testing will occur. 
- The MSA must approve the testing and the plan (tacit approval after 30 days unless national law requires an explicit authorisation).
- The testing must be registered in the EU database with a Union‑wide unique single identification number (with specific registration routes/exceptions depending on the Annex III category/area).
- The provider/prospective provider must be established in the Union or appoint an EU‑established legal representative.
- Transfers of data collected/processed for the test to third countries are allowed only with appropriate and applicable Union‑law safeguards.
- Duration must be no longer than necessary and in any case no more than 6 months (extendable once by up to 6 months with prior notification and justification to the MSA).
- Vulnerable subjects (due to age or disability) must be appropriately protected.
- If testing is done with deployers/prospective deployers: they must be informed of relevant aspects, given relevant instructions for use, and an agreement must allocate roles/responsibilities to ensure compliance.
- Subjects must give informed consent (per Article 61); for law enforcement where consent would prevent testing, the test/outcome must not negatively affect subjects and their personal data must be deleted after the test.
- Testing must be effectively overseen by suitably qualified persons with necessary capacity/training/authority.
- The system’s outputs must be effectively reversible/disregardable.

Separately, the Act also indicates that “testing in real‑world conditions” may be included in accordance with Article 60.

bench:qa:57.answer_text:
For real‑world testing, the Act requires that the **subjects of the testing in real‑world conditions give informed consent in accordance with Article 61**.

If the testing is **in the context of law enforcement** and **seeking informed consent would prevent the AI system from being tested**, informed consent is not required, but two safeguards must apply instead: **(1) the testing itself and its outcome must not have any negative effect on the subjects**, and **(2) the subjects’ personal data must be deleted after the test is performed**.

(“Subjects” here are the natural persons participating in the real‑world testing.)

bench:qa:58.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act provisions provided, affected (natural) persons have a right to be informed when they are subject to the use of certain high‑risk AI systems that make or assist in making decisions about them.

- **Right to be informed of use**: Deployers of Annex III high‑risk AI systems that make decisions or assist in making decisions related to natural persons **must inform those natural persons** that they are subject to the use of the high‑risk AI system. (For high‑risk AI systems used for law enforcement purposes, the information duty is governed instead by Article 13 of Directive (EU) 2016/680.)

bench:qa:59.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain the penalty amounts or types of sanctions for non‑compliance with prohibited AI practices.

They do indicate that, in the context of market surveillance notifications, authorities must specify when a case involves “non‑compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5.”

bench:qa:60.answer_text: For breaches of operator (or notified body) obligations other than prohibited practices under Article 5, the maximum administrative fine is up to EUR 15,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year—whichever is higher.

bench:qa:61.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain any provisions on administrative fines or how fines are adjusted for SMEs and start-ups. They cover SME/start-up support measures (e.g., priority access to regulatory sandboxes, training and advice channels, participation in standardisation, and taking SME needs into account for codes of conduct) and a simplification option for technical documentation, but nothing about fine calculation, reductions, caps, or adjustments.

So, based only on the supplied context, the adjustment of fines for SMEs/start-ups cannot be determined.

bench:qa:62.answer_text:
Under Article 99, when competent authorities exercise their powers to impose administrative fines, that exercise must be subject to appropriate procedural safeguards in accordance with Union and national law. Those safeguards must include effective judicial remedies and due process.

In addition, Member States must lay down rules on the extent to which administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State.

bench:qa:63.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, market-surveillance authorities have a supervisory and enforcement-facing role in relation to AI systems, including:

- Receiving incident and risk-related notifications: providers must report any serious incident involving high-risk AI systems to the market-surveillance authorities of the Member State where it occurred, and providers must inform the competent market-surveillance authorities when they become aware that a high-risk AI system presents a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)). Importers must also inform market-surveillance authorities (along with the provider and authorised representative) where a high-risk AI system presents such a risk. 

- Receiving information and documentation relevant to oversight: authorised representatives must provide a copy of their mandate to market-surveillance authorities upon request; and notified bodies must record/track requests for information they receive from market-surveillance authorities regarding conformity-assessment activities.

- Supervising AI regulatory sandboxes: where real-world testing is conducted for AI systems supervised within an AI regulatory sandbox, market-surveillance authorities must verify compliance with Article 60 as part of their supervisory role, and may in certain cases allow testing to be conducted by the provider/prospective provider in derogation from some Article 60(4) conditions.

- Receiving deployer reporting for certain biometric identification uses: deployers must submit annual reports to the relevant market-surveillance (and national data protection) authorities on their use of post-remote biometric identification systems (with an exception for sensitive operational law-enforcement data).

- Participating in coordinated and cross-border market surveillance: EU-level bodies may support joint and cross-border market-surveillance activities, while preserving market-surveillance authorities’ powers, and may support the work of market-surveillance authorities at their request.

- Institutional context: for AI systems put into service or used by Union institutions, agencies, offices and bodies, references to national competent authorities or market-surveillance authorities are to be read as references to the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS).

bench:qa:64.answer_text:
A market‑surveillance authority can intervene on certificates in two situations reflected in the provided provisions:

1) **If it finds a high‑risk AI system is non‑compliant during a risk evaluation**: where the authority has sufficient reason to consider an AI system presents a risk and, in the course of its evaluation, **finds the system does not comply** with the Regulation’s requirements/obligations, it must require corrective actions (including withdrawal/recall of the system) and **inform the relevant notified body accordingly**. (This provision does not itself say “suspend/withdraw the certificate”, but it is the trigger for notifying the notified body in the non‑compliance scenario.)

2) **If certificates were “unduly issued”**: the authority may **require the notified body to suspend or withdraw, within a reasonable period set by the authority, any certificates which were unduly issued**, to ensure continuing conformity of high‑risk AI systems on the market.

bench:qa:65.answer_text:
Under Article 47(3), where a high-risk AI system is also subject to other Union harmonisation legislation that requires an EU declaration of conformity and a single declaration is drawn up for all applicable Union law, the EU declaration of conformity must contain **all the information required to identify the Union harmonisation legislation to which the declaration relates**.

The provided excerpts do not specify any additional mandatory content elements beyond this identification information (they otherwise refer to drawing up/keeping a copy of the declaration).

bench:qa:66.answer_text:
For high‑risk AI systems, the CE marking is the marking by which the provider indicates that the system is in conformity with the requirements of the EU AI Act (specifically the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2) and with any other applicable Union harmonisation legislation that provides for CE marking.

If the high‑risk AI system is also subject to other Union law that provides for CE marking, the CE marking also indicates that the system fulfils the requirements of that other law.

bench:qa:67.answer_text:
The provisions provided do not set a specific date or deadline by which providers of general‑purpose AI models must comply with the AI Office’s codes of practice.

Instead, adherence to (approved) codes of practice is presented as voluntary (“may invite … to adhere”), and as an optional way to demonstrate compliance with the underlying legal obligations (Articles 53(1) and 55(1)) until harmonised standards are published. If a provider does not adhere to an approved code of practice (or does not comply with a harmonised standard), it must demonstrate “alternative adequate means of compliance” for assessment by the Commission.

bench:qa:68.answer_text: Under Article 72(3), the Commission’s post‑market monitoring plan template is intended to set out detailed provisions that establish a standard template for the post‑market monitoring plan and specify the list of elements that must be included in that plan (which the post‑market monitoring system must be based on and which forms part of the technical documentation).

bench:qa:69.answer_text:
From the provided excerpts, there is no exemption for a provider from the obligation to have a quality management system (QMS) in place. Providers of high-risk AI systems “shall have a quality management system in place which complies with Article 17.”

The only flexibility shown is that where providers are already subject to quality-management-system (or equivalent) obligations under relevant sectoral Union law, they may incorporate (“include”) the Article 17(1) aspects into the quality management system required under that sectoral law—this is not an exemption from having a QMS, but an integration option.

No other provider exemption conditions are included in the supplied context.

bench:qa:70.answer_text: If a substantial modification is made to a high‑risk AI system, the system must undergo a new conformity assessment procedure. In addition, the party that makes the substantial modification (e.g., a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party) is treated as the “provider” of that high‑risk AI system and is therefore subject to the provider obligations under Article 16.

bench:qa:71.answer_text:
If a serious incident involves the death of a person, it qualifies as a “serious incident” under the Act and must be reported as such.

For certain Annex III high-risk AI systems placed on the market/put into service by providers already subject to equivalent Union-law reporting regimes, the AI Act limits the required notification of serious incidents to those falling under the fundamental-rights category (Article 3(49)(c)), rather than all categories of “serious incident.”

In general, the reporting period must take account of the severity of the serious incident.

Providers must also have procedures in place for reporting serious incidents in accordance with Article 73.

bench:qa:72.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not specify any timeframe for a market-surveillance authority to object to a notified body’s designation. The cited provisions address (i) changes/cessation of a notified body’s activities and related information duties (Article 36(3), 36(9)), (ii) file-keeping when a designation is restricted/suspended/withdrawn (Article 36(6)), and (iii) market surveillance evaluations and corrective-action deadlines for non-compliant AI systems (Article 79(2)), but none set a deadline for an objection to a designation.

bench:qa:73.answer_text:
A provider can rely on a presumption of conformity when it complies with European harmonised standards, but only to the extent those standards cover the relevant obligations/requirements.

In the provisions provided here, this is stated explicitly for providers of general-purpose AI models (including those with systemic risk): compliance with European harmonised standards grants a presumption of conformity insofar as the standards cover the obligations in question (and, until a harmonised standard is published, providers may instead rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance).

bench:qa:75.answer_text:
In AI regulatory sandboxes, the AI Office has a support-and-coordination role.

- National competent authorities must inform the AI Office when they establish a sandbox and may request the AI Office’s support and guidance. The AI Office must also publish and keep updated a public list of planned and existing sandboxes to encourage interaction and cross-border cooperation. 
- In addition, cooperation structures are tasked with assisting the AI Office in supporting national competent authorities in establishing and developing sandboxes, and in facilitating cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes.

bench:qa:76.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain any obligations specifically addressed to “downstream providers” in relation to high‑risk AI systems.

In the material you supplied, the only explicit rule about downstream providers is that they have a right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of the Regulation (this is a right, not an obligation).

bench:qa:77.answer_text: Its purpose is to assess the impact on fundamental rights that the use of a high‑risk AI system may produce, and—where relevant—serve as a complement to an existing data protection impact assessment (DPIA) if DPIA obligations already cover parts of the required assessment.

bench:qa:78.answer_text: Deployers must inform the provider **immediately** when they have identified a serious incident (and then inform the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities).

bench:qa:79.answer_text: Testing of high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions must not last longer than necessary to achieve its objectives and, in any case, not longer than six months. It may be extended once for an additional six months, subject to prior notification to the market surveillance authority with an explanation of the need for the extension. Therefore, the maximum duration is 12 months (6 months + one 6-month extension).

bench:qa:80.answer_text:
Market‑surveillance authorities (and national competent authorities when performing their tasks) must handle information and documentation they obtain under the AI Act in line with the confidentiality obligations laid down in Article 78.

In particular:
- When performing their tasks, national competent authorities must act in accordance with the confidentiality obligations set out in Article 78.
- Any information or documentation obtained by market‑surveillance authorities must be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations set out in Article 78.

bench:qa:81.answer_text:
If a market‑surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider an AI system presents a risk, it must evaluate the system’s compliance with all requirements and obligations under the Regulation (with particular attention to risks to vulnerable groups). If risks to fundamental rights are identified, it must also inform and fully cooperate with the relevant national public authorities/bodies, and operators must cooperate as necessary. 

Following that evaluation:
- If the authority finds non‑compliance, it must, without undue delay, require the relevant operator to take appropriate corrective actions to bring the system into compliance, or to withdraw or recall it, within a period the authority prescribes (and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period provided by relevant Union harmonisation legislation). It must also inform the relevant notified body. 
- If the authority finds that a high‑risk AI system complies with the Regulation but nevertheless presents a risk to health/safety, fundamental rights, or other public‑interest protection aspects, it must require the relevant operator to take all appropriate measures so that, when placed on the market or put into service, the system no longer presents that risk, without undue delay and within a period the authority may prescribe.

bench:qa:82.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, providers’ accessibility-related obligations are:

- Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements, in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.

- Where a provider of a high-risk AI system is already subject to obligations regarding quality management systems (or an equivalent function) under relevant sectoral Union law, the provider may integrate the relevant AI Act quality-management aspects into that existing quality management system.

(Separately from providers’ obligations, the Act also requires the EU database to comply with applicable accessibility requirements.)

bench:qa:83.answer_text: A provider must draw up an EU declaration of conformity (in accordance with Article 47) for each high‑risk AI system. The cited provisions do not specify a precise moment (e.g., “before placing on the market/putting into service”) for drawing it up; they only require that it be drawn up and then kept available to national competent authorities for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service.

bench:qa:84.answer_text:
For AI systems put into service or used by Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) takes on the roles that the Act otherwise assigns to national competent authorities and market surveillance authorities.

Concretely:
- The EDPS acts as the competent authority for supervising Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies that fall within the scope of the Regulation. 
- The EDPS also acts as their market surveillance authority (with an exception for the Court of Justice of the EU when acting in its judicial capacity). 
- In EDPS proceedings concerning possible infringements, the EDPS must give the Union institution/body/office/agency concerned an opportunity to be heard before taking a decision, and must base decisions only on elements and circumstances on which the parties have been able to comment; complainants (if any) are to be closely associated with the proceedings.

bench:qa:85.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, there is no standalone obligation for providers to submit periodic “reports” specifically about the post‑market monitoring plan. The Act does, however, impose documentation/availability obligations tied to the plan:

- Providers’ post‑market monitoring system must be based on a post‑market monitoring plan, and that plan must be included as part of the technical documentation (Annex IV). This effectively requires providers to document the plan within the technical documentation set. 
- Annex IV further specifies that the technical documentation must contain a detailed description of the post‑market performance evaluation system, including the post‑market monitoring plan.

Separately (not a provider reporting duty), the Commission must adopt an implementing act establishing a template and required elements for the plan by 2 February 2026.

If you meant “reporting” in the sense of incident reporting (e.g., serious incidents), that is governed by other provisions (e.g., Article 73), which are not included here beyond a limited excerpt and do not set out plan-specific reporting duties in this context.

bench:qa:86.answer_text: If the scientific panel makes a duly substantiated request, the Commission may send a request for information to a provider of a general-purpose AI model. In that case, the provider must provide the requested information to the Commission, but only insofar as access to that information is necessary and proportionate for the scientific panel to fulfil its tasks under Article 68(2).

bench:qa:87.answer_text: For high-risk AI systems related to products covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, a provider can be exempt (derogate) from the EU AI Act conformity‑assessment procedure only where, and to the extent that, an exemption/derogation from conformity assessment is already established in the applicable Union harmonisation legislation for that product. No additional or separate exemptions are created by the AI Act for those product-related high-risk AI systems.

bench:qa:88.answer_text:
The excerpts you provided do not include the AI Act’s general “dates of application” (the transitional/applicability provisions). They only state obligations that apply **before** placing on the market/putting into service/using a **high‑risk AI system listed in Annex III** (with an exception for Annex III point 2), such as registration in the EU database.

So, based only on this context, the specific calendar date when the Regulation becomes applicable to Annex III high‑risk AI systems cannot be determined.

bench:qa:89.answer_text: The AI Office’s codes of practice (at Union level) are intended to facilitate the effective implementation of the Regulation’s obligations on detecting and labelling artificially generated or manipulated content. More generally, they serve as a voluntary framework that the AI Office can invite providers of general‑purpose AI models to adhere to, and the AI Office can monitor providers’ compliance with the Regulation including their adherence to approved codes of practice.

bench:qa:90.answer_text: Providers must ensure that the technical solutions used to ensure the cybersecurity of high‑risk AI systems are appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

bench:qa:91.answer_text:
Providers’ obligations regarding logs vis-à-vis competent authorities are:

- Keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems (the logs referred to in Article 12(1)) to the extent those logs are under their control. Those logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system and for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (in particular data protection law). 

- Upon a reasoned request by a competent authority, give the requesting competent authority access to the automatically generated logs of the high-risk AI system (Article 12(1) logs), to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

- Upon a reasoned request, provide a competent authority with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity of a high-risk AI system with Section 2 requirements, including access to the automatically generated logs (Article 12(1) logs), to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

bench:qa:92.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not include the EU AI Act’s penalty provisions for non-compliance by providers of general-purpose AI models, so the maximum fine cannot be determined from the supplied context.

bench:qa:93.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must conduct adversarial testing as part of its obligation to perform model evaluation in accordance with state‑of‑the‑art standardised protocols and tools. That model evaluation must include conducting and documenting adversarial testing, with the aim of identifying and mitigating systemic risks.

bench:qa:94.answer_text: In the Union safeguard procedure, the AI Office’s role is to be supported by the European Artificial Intelligence Board (or its relevant structures) in carrying out the AI Office’s duties under that procedure (pursuant to Article 81).

bench:qa:95.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not specify what information must be included in the EU database entry for law‑enforcement related high‑risk AI systems.

They only state that, for “real‑time” remote biometric identification systems used in publicly accessible spaces for law‑enforcement purposes, use must be authorised only if the law‑enforcement authority has registered the system in the EU database according to Article 49 (with a limited urgency exception allowing use before registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay).

bench:qa:96.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems have to have/put in place a quality management system (QMS) that complies with Article 17 and ensures compliance with the Regulation. The QMS must include at least techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system. Providers must keep the documentation concerning that QMS at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service. Where providers are already subject to sectoral Union-law obligations on QMS (or an equivalent function), they may integrate the Article 17(1) aspects into the QMS required under that sectoral law.

bench:qa:97.answer_text:
A market‑surveillance authority can issue a provisional suspension (i.e., “appropriate provisional measures” to prohibit or restrict making the AI system available or putting it into service, or to withdraw/recall it) when:

1) It has evaluated an AI system because it has sufficient reason to consider it presents a risk, and it has required the relevant operator to take corrective action within a prescribed period (in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period provided by relevant Union harmonisation legislation); and

2) The operator does not take adequate corrective action within that period.

In that case, the authority must take those provisional measures and notify the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay.

bench:qa:98.answer_text: The purpose of the AI Office’s single information platform is to provide easy-to-use information about the Regulation for all operators across the Union.

bench:qa:99.answer_text:
If a serious incident occurs during real‑world testing, the provider must:

- Report the serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State(s) where the incident occurred (for providers of high‑risk AI systems placed on the Union market). The report must be made immediately after the provider has established a causal link (or a reasonable likelihood of such a link) between the AI system and the incident, and in any event no later than 15 days after the provider (or, where applicable, the deployer) becomes aware of the incident.
- Following that reporting, carry out the necessary investigations into the serious incident and the AI system concerned, without delay.

Separately (as part of the real‑world testing regime), providers/prospective providers must notify the national market surveillance authority of any suspension or termination of the real‑world testing and of the final outcomes.

bench:qa:100.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, there is no general rule saying that a provider may “use a free and open‑source AI model without an authorised representative”. The only explicit authorised‑representative condition in your context is that (for high‑risk AI systems) importers must verify that “the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1)”.

What the Act does provide (in your excerpts) are *free and open‑source* exceptions to certain obligations, but these are not framed as an exemption from appointing an authorised representative:

- For certain obligations on providers of AI models (Article 53(1)(a) and (b)), those obligations do not apply if the model is released under a free and open‑source licence that allows access/usage/modification/distribution and the model’s parameters (including weights), architecture information, and usage information are publicly available; however, this exception does not apply to general‑purpose AI models with systemic risks. 
- For the obligation in Article 54, it does not apply to providers of general‑purpose AI models released under such a free and open‑source licence with publicly available parameters/architecture/usage information, unless the model presents systemic risks.
- Separately, the Regulation generally does not apply to AI systems released under free and open‑source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high‑risk AI systems or as an AI system falling under Article 5 or 50.

So, based only on the cited text, the “conditions” you can point to relate to when certain obligations (or the Regulation itself) do not apply for free/open‑source releases, and the importer verification requirement for high‑risk systems; the excerpts do not establish a condition under which an authorised representative is not needed solely because a model is free/open‑source.

bench:qa:101.answer_text: Deployers who are employers must inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers **before** putting into service or using a high‑risk AI system at the workplace (with the information provided, where applicable, in accordance with applicable Union and national rules and procedures on informing workers and their representatives).

bench:qa:102.answer_text: 10 years after the system has been placed on the market (or put into service, for high-risk AI systems).

bench:qa:103.answer_text: Importers must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, the system’s storage or transport conditions (where applicable) do not jeopardise its compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2.

bench:qa:104.answer_text: If a provider considers or has reason to consider that a high‑risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation, it must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, as appropriate, to: (i) bring the system into conformity, or (ii) withdraw it, or (iii) disable it, or (iv) recall it. The provider must also inform the distributors of the system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers accordingly.

bench:qa:105.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, the European Artificial Intelligence Board must establish two standing sub-groups whose role is to serve as platforms for cooperation and exchange:

- A standing sub-group for cooperation among market surveillance authorities on issues related to market surveillance; this sub-group should act as the Administrative Cooperation Group (ADCO) for the Regulation.
- A standing sub-group for cooperation among notifying authorities on issues related to notified bodies.

In addition, the Board may set up other standing or temporary sub-groups to examine specific issues, and (where appropriate) representatives of the advisory forum may be invited to these sub-groups or meetings as observers. The Board’s rules of procedure must also organise the Board’s activities and those of its sub-groups, including specifying aspects such as the organisation of sub-group activities.

bench:qa:106.answer_text:
A provider can rely on a code of practice (code of conduct) to demonstrate compliance for a general‑purpose AI model only **until a harmonised standard is published**, and only **to demonstrate compliance with the specific obligations referenced in the relevant article**:

- **General‑purpose AI models (non‑systemic risk):** providers may rely on codes of practice (within the meaning of Article 56) to demonstrate compliance with the **obligations in Article 53(1)**, **until a harmonised standard is published**. If they do not adhere to an approved code of practice or do not comply with a European harmonised standard, they must demonstrate **alternative adequate means of compliance** for assessment by the Commission. 

- **General‑purpose AI models with systemic risk:** providers may rely on codes of practice (within the meaning of Article 56) to demonstrate compliance with the **obligations in Article 55(1)**, **until a harmonised standard is published**. If they do not adhere to an approved code of practice or do not comply with a European harmonised standard, they must demonstrate **alternative adequate means of compliance** for assessment by the Commission.

bench:qa:107.answer_text: The purpose of the AI Office’s evaluation of systemic risks is to identify and support the mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level arising from general-purpose AI models with systemic risk—i.e., risks stemming from their development, placing on the market, or use—based on model evaluation (including adversarial testing) and related evaluation strategies/results that surface limitations and risks so they can be addressed.

bench:qa:108.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain any operative obligation requiring providers of general‑purpose AI models to provide a “summary of training data.” The only general‑purpose AI model provision included here (Article 53(4)) concerns how providers may demonstrate compliance with obligations in Article 53(1) (via codes of practice, harmonised standards, or alternative adequate means), but the underlying obligations in Article 53(1)—including any possible requirement about a training‑data summary—are not included in the context.

Therefore, based only on the supplied text, no specific “summary of training data” duty can be stated.

bench:qa:109.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system to indicate conformity with the Regulation, in accordance with Article 48. If affixing it to the system is not possible, the provider must affix the CE marking on the packaging or on the accompanying documentation (also in accordance with Article 48).

bench:qa:110.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must report relevant information about serious incidents **without undue delay** (to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities).

bench:qa:111.answer_text: The maximum fine for non‑compliance with the prohibition of AI practices (Article 5) is up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

bench:qa:112.answer_text: The AI Office’s codes of practice are intended to foster the voluntary application of specific AI Act requirements and thereby contribute to the proper application of the Regulation. In particular, they are meant to foster the voluntary application (to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems) of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices, and more generally to contribute to the proper application of the Regulation (taking into account international approaches).

bench:qa:113.answer_text: For **high-risk AI systems** (other than those covered by Article 111(1)) that were **placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026**, the Regulation applies **only if, from 2 August 2026, those systems are subject to significant changes in their design**. Separately, **providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities** must in any case **take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2030**.

bench:qa:114.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, providers’ obligation regarding EU database registration is to comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1). Failure to carry out the required registration in the EU database can be treated as an infringement (the Act refers to cases where “the registration in the EU database … has not been carried out”).

Relatedly, where an authorised representative is involved, it must (where applicable) comply with the same registration obligations, or—if the provider carries out the registration itself—ensure the correctness of the relevant Annex VIII information.

bench:qa:115.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, the AI Office supports AI regulatory sandboxes mainly by:

- Being a point of support and guidance for national competent authorities: authorities must inform the AI Office when they establish a sandbox and may ask the AI Office for support and guidance. (eu-ai-act:article-57:paragraph-15)

- Increasing transparency and enabling cross-border interaction: the AI Office must publish and keep up to date a public list of planned and existing sandboxes, to encourage more interaction among sandboxes and cross-border cooperation. (eu-ai-act:article-57:paragraph-15)

- Supporting the establishment and development of sandboxes and cooperation between them (as part of the broader governance setup): the Act provides for assisting the AI Office in supporting national competent authorities in establishing and developing sandboxes, and facilitating cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes. (eu-ai-act:article-66:paragraph-1:point-k)

bench:qa:116.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain any operative provision specifying **when** a provider of a general‑purpose AI model must notify the Commission about a **systemic‑risk classification** (e.g., a deadline such as “without undue delay” or a number of days).

The only timing-related notification duty to the Commission in the supplied context concerns **serious incidents** (“immediately notify … the Commission of any serious incident”), which is not the same as notifying systemic‑risk classification.

bench:qa:117.answer_text:
For high-risk AI systems, providers’ post‑market monitoring obligations imply that they must have a post‑market monitoring plan because:

- The provider must establish and document a post‑market monitoring system (proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high‑risk AI system). That system must be based on a post‑market monitoring plan. 
- The post‑market monitoring plan must be included as part of the technical documentation (Annex IV technical documentation includes the post‑market monitoring plan).

In addition, where a post‑market monitoring system and plan are already established under certain Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), providers may integrate the necessary elements using the Commission template to ensure consistency and avoid duplication, provided an equivalent level of protection is achieved.

bench:qa:118.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, market‑surveillance authorities are to be granted access to the source code of a high‑risk AI system only upon a reasoned request and only where both conditions are met: (1) access to source code is necessary to assess conformity with the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2; and (2) testing/auditing and verifications based on the data and documentation provided by the provider have been exhausted or proved insufficient.

The provisions you provided do not add any further specific procedural duty on providers beyond the fact that access is granted under those conditions.

bench:qa:119.answer_text: Under the Act, the scientific panel is intended to support enforcement activities. The AI Office’s scientific panel alerts are therefore part of that support function: they are “qualified alerts” that must be duly reasoned and include at least the provider’s point of contact, a description of the relevant facts and the reasons for the alert, and any other information the panel considers relevant (including information gathered on its own initiative). The detailed conditions and procedures for issuing such alerts (and for the panel to request AI Office assistance) are to be set out in an implementing act.

bench:qa:120.answer_text: For a high-risk AI system that is related to a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, a provider can only rely on (and thus be exempt from) the conformity-assessment procedure to the extent that the relevant Union harmonisation legislation itself provides a derogation from conformity assessment. The AI Act does not create additional or separate exemptions for those product-related high-risk AI systems beyond those derogations.

bench:qa:121.answer_text:
From the provisions provided in your context, there is no explicit obligation stated that requires providers of general‑purpose AI models to provide a “summary of training data” (or a “summary about the content used for training”), nor any described content, format, timing, or recipient for such a summary.

The only relevant statement in the supplied text is that codes of practice may address “the adequate level of detail for the summary about the content used for training,” but that provision does not itself impose a direct provider obligation to produce or provide such a summary.

bench:qa:122.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not specify any maximum duration for how long a sandbox plan may be in effect. They only define that a sandbox plan includes a “timeframe” and that certain logs are kept “for the duration of the participation in the sandbox,” but no maximum time limit is stated here.

bench:qa:123.answer_text: If a high‑risk AI system continues to learn after being placed on the market/put into service, it must be developed so as to (i) eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of biased outputs feeding back into future inputs (feedback loops) and (ii) ensure those feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures. In addition, if post‑market learning results in a **substantial modification**, the system must undergo a **new conformity assessment**; however, changes and performance updates that were **pre‑determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment** and included in the technical documentation do **not** count as a substantial modification (so they do not trigger a new conformity assessment on that basis).

bench:qa:124.answer_text: A provider must keep the logs (referred to in Article 12(1)) automatically generated by its high‑risk AI system for a period appropriate to the system’s intended purpose, and in any event for at least six months, to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control. This minimum retention applies unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (in particular Union law on personal data protection).

bench:qa:125.answer_text: For AI systems put into service or used by Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) acts as the competent authority responsible for their supervision. In that context, references in the Regulation to “national competent authorities” or “market surveillance authorities” are to be read as references to the EDPS. The EDPS may also establish an AI regulatory sandbox for Union institutions and may exercise the roles and tasks of national competent authorities under the sandbox chapter. When conducting proceedings and before taking decisions, the EDPS must give the Union institution/body/office/agency concerned an opportunity to be heard, base decisions only on elements the parties could comment on, and closely associate complainants (if any) with the proceedings.

bench:qa:126.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, CE marking obligations for providers relate to **high-risk AI systems**:

- **Affix the CE marking to indicate conformity with the Regulation**: Providers must affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system to indicate conformity with the Regulation, in accordance with Article 48. If affixing it on the system is not possible, it must be affixed on the packaging or accompanying documentation. 

- **Meaning/effect of the CE marking**: The CE marking is the marking by which the provider indicates that the AI system is in conformity with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 and other applicable Union harmonisation legislation providing for its affixing.

- **Where other Union law also requires CE marking**: If the high-risk AI system is subject to other Union law that also provides for CE marking, the CE marking must indicate that the system also fulfils the requirements of that other law.

(Separately, importers and distributors have verification duties before placing/making available high-risk AI systems, but the provider’s core obligation is to affix the CE marking as above.)

bench:qa:127.answer_text: In the event of a serious incident involving the death of a person, the provider must provide the report to the market‑surveillance authority **immediately after** it has established, or as soon as it suspects, a causal relationship between the high‑risk AI system and the serious incident, and **in any case no later than 10 days** after the date on which the provider becomes aware of the serious incident.

bench:qa:128.answer_text: The purpose of the AI Office’s (i.e., the Commission’s) guidelines on the practical implementation of the Regulation is to provide practical guidance on how to apply and implement the Regulation in key areas, in particular: (a) applying the requirements and obligations in Articles 8–15 and Article 25; (b) applying the prohibited practices in Article 5; (c) implementing the rules on substantial modification; (d) implementing the transparency obligations in Article 50; (e) explaining the relationship with Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and other relevant Union law (including consistency in enforcement); and (f) applying the definition of an AI system in Article 3(1). In addition, when issuing the guidelines, the Commission must pay particular attention to the needs of SMEs (including start-ups), local public authorities, and sectors most likely to be affected, and the guidelines must take due account of the state of the art and relevant harmonised standards/common specifications. Separately, for Article 6 specifically, the Commission must also provide guidelines on its practical implementation together with a comprehensive list of practical examples of use cases of AI systems that are high-risk and not high-risk.

bench:qa:129.answer_text: From the provisions provided, there is no explicit rule stating when a market‑surveillance authority may suspend a high‑risk AI system “without prior notice”. The cited AI Act provisions here describe (i) the authority’s duty to evaluate systems it considers risky and, if non‑compliance is found, to require corrective actions/withdrawal/recall within set deadlines, with Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applying to those measures, and (ii) that notification procedures must be followed as provided in that Regulation. Any possibility of acting without prior notice would therefore depend on the applicable procedures under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 (not included in the provided excerpts), rather than being specified directly in the provided AI Act text.

bench:qa:130.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk AI systems have the following obligations regarding a post-market monitoring system:

- Establish and document a post-market monitoring system, in a way proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system. 
- Ensure the post-market monitoring system is based on a post-market monitoring plan.
- Include the post-market monitoring plan in the technical documentation (Annex IV).
- As part of the provider’s quality management system, cover the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of the post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72.
- Put in place a system (described in the technical documentation) to evaluate the AI system’s performance in the post-market phase in accordance with Article 72, including the post-market monitoring plan.
- Ensure the system’s logging/recording capabilities facilitate the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72.

bench:qa:131.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain a specific obligation on providers that is triggered by a notified body withdrawing a certificate.

From the cited provisions, the only directly relevant provider duties involving a notified body are:
- If the provider becomes aware that a high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the provider must (where applicable) inform the notified body that issued the certificate. 
- If the provider intends to introduce (or becomes aware of) changes to the AI system that could affect compliance or intended purpose, the provider must inform the notified body that issued the relevant certificate so the notified body can assess the changes.

None of the cited text addresses what the provider must do specifically “if a notified body withdraws a certificate.”

bench:qa:132.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must conduct adversarial testing as part of its obligation to perform model evaluation in accordance with state‑of‑the‑art standardised protocols and tools. The adversarial testing must be conducted and documented, with the aim of identifying and mitigating systemic risks.

bench:qa:133.answer_text: From the provided excerpts, the maximum fine amount is not stated. The Act excerpt indicates that fines for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information are “provided for in Article 101,” but the specific maximum level is not included in the text you supplied.

bench:qa:134.answer_text:
Providers must affix the CE marking to their high‑risk AI system to indicate conformity with the Regulation, in accordance with Article 48. If affixing it on the system is not possible, they must affix it on the packaging or accompanying documentation.

Where the high‑risk AI system is also subject to other Union law that provides for CE marking, the CE marking must indicate that the system also fulfils the requirements of that other Union law.

bench:qa:0.answer_text: Based on the provided provisions, the Regulation’s primary purpose is to ensure and assess compliance with its requirements—i.e., that AI systems (including high-risk systems and general-purpose AI models) conform to the Regulation and that authorities can obtain information needed to assess such compliance.

bench:qa:1.answer_text:
Based on the provisions provided, the following actors have obligations under the AI Regulation and therefore must comply with the relevant requirements that apply to them:

- Providers of high-risk AI systems (including compliance with registration obligations in Article 49(1)).
- Providers who consider that an AI system listed in Annex III is not high-risk (they must document their assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service).
- Authorised representatives (where applicable, including registration obligations in Article 49(1)).
- Deployers (including obligations such as assigning human oversight).
- Deployers of high-risk AI systems that are public authorities (or Union institutions/bodies/offices/agencies), including registration/database-related obligations.
- Deployers who are employers using a high-risk AI system at the workplace (they must inform workers’ representatives and affected workers).
- Providers of general-purpose AI models (indirectly reflected via obligations on others to take measures to comply with Articles 53 and 54, and requirements intended to enable providers of AI systems to comply with their obligations).

This is not an exhaustive list of all addressees in the Regulation; it reflects only the obligations contained in the excerpts you provided.

bench:qa:2.answer_text: Generally, no—where an AI system is placed on the market, put into service, or used (with or without modification) **exclusively** for military, defence or national security purposes, the EU AI Act **does not apply**, regardless of what type of entity is carrying out those activities. The Regulation also states it does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law and does not affect Member States’ competences concerning national security. In addition, if an AI system is **not** placed on the market or put into service in the Union, but its output is used in the Union **exclusively** for military/defence/national security purposes, the Regulation also does not apply.

bench:qa:3.answer_text: Under the Regulation, an ‘AI system’ means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs (such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions) that can influence physical or virtual environments.

bench:qa:4.answer_text: Under the AI Act, an AI system “presenting a risk” is understood as a “product presenting a risk” (within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020) insofar as the AI system presents risks to persons’ health or safety, or to their fundamental rights.

bench:qa:5.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, the Act does not give a general definition of “provider” of an AI system. However, it specifies that certain actors are to be treated as a “provider” (of a high-risk AI system) for the purposes of the Regulation.

In particular, **any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party** is **considered a provider of a high-risk AI system** where, in any of these circumstances:
- they **put their name or trademark** on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service;
- they **make a substantial modification** to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market/put into service, such that it remains high-risk; or
- they **modify the intended purpose** of an AI system (including a general-purpose AI system) that was not high-risk and was already placed on the market/put into service, so that it becomes high-risk.

Separately, the Act refers to “a provider” as the actor who places or puts into service an AI system and, for example, must document an assessment when they consider an Annex III system is not high-risk, before placing it on the market or putting it into service.

bench:qa:6.answer_text: In the AI Regulation, a “deployer” is the actor expected to use (deploy) an AI system in practice—particularly a high-risk AI system—so that the system’s design and risk controls must take into account the deployer’s expected technical knowledge, experience, education and training, as well as the context in which the system is intended to be used.

bench:qa:7.answer_text:
The excerpts you provided do not contain a standalone, general obligation on providers and deployers to ensure or provide “AI literacy” (e.g., training/competence measures) as such.

What they do contain is:
- A definition of “AI literacy”: it is the skills, knowledge and understanding enabling providers, deployers and affected persons—taking into account their rights and obligations under the Regulation—to make an informed deployment of AI systems and to be aware of opportunities, risks and possible harm. 
- For high-risk AI systems, the provider must ensure the provision to deployers of the information required under Article 13 and, where appropriate, training (this is the closest operational requirement in your context that relates to literacy/competence).

Separately, the context also mentions “promoting AI literacy” as an objective/activity, but it is not framed here as a direct duty on providers/deployers.

bench:qa:8.answer_text: The provided context does not include any of the specific prohibited AI practices listed in Article 5 (it only references that such prohibited practices exist).

bench:qa:9.answer_text:
Yes, but only in narrowly limited circumstances and subject to strict conditions.

The Act allows Member States to provide for the possibility to (fully or partially) authorise the use of “real-time” remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, but only within the limits and conditions set out in Article 5(1)(h) and Article 5(2)–(3). Where used, it must be only to confirm the identity of a specifically targeted individual, must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards (including temporal, geographic and personal limitations) under national law, and may be authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment and registered the system in the EU database (with a limited urgency exception for registration).

bench:qa:10.answer_text: Under Article 6, an AI system is classified as a “high‑risk AI system” when it meets the conditions in Article 6(1): it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product (or the AI system as a product) is required to undergo a third‑party conformity assessment under that Annex I legislation before being placed on the market or put into service (this applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market/put into service independently of the product).

bench:qa:11.answer_text:
Yes—under a limited derogation.

An AI system referred to in Annex III can be treated as not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights (including by not materially influencing decision-making) and one of the listed conditions in Article 6(3) is met (e.g., narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting patterns without replacing/influencing prior human assessment without proper human review, or a preparatory task). However, an Annex III system must always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons.

If a provider considers an Annex III system not high-risk, it must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, and must provide that documentation to national competent authorities upon request. A market surveillance authority may evaluate whether a system classified by the provider as non-high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3) is in fact high-risk.

bench:qa:12.answer_text: According to Article 8(1), high‑risk AI systems shall comply with the requirements laid down in this Section, taking into account their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI‑related technologies. When ensuring compliance with those requirements, the risk management system referred to in Article 9 shall be taken into account.

bench:qa:13.answer_text:
Under Article 9, the risk management system for high-risk AI systems is a continuous, iterative process run throughout the entire lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating. It comprises these main steps:

1) Identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when used as intended.
2) Estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge when used as intended and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse.
3) Evaluate other risks possibly arising, based on data from the post-market monitoring system.
4) Adopt appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified.

In addition, high-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures, and to ensure consistent performance for the intended purpose and compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

The risk management system must be established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems. Where providers are already subject to internal risk management processes under other Union law, the Article 9 aspects may be part of, or combined with, those procedures.

bench:qa:14.answer_text: Under Article 10, high‑risk AI systems that use training techniques must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet the Act’s quality criteria. In particular, those data sets must be: (1) relevant; (2) sufficiently representative; (3) to the best extent possible, free of errors; (4) complete in view of the intended purpose; and (5) have appropriate statistical properties (including, where applicable, regarding the persons or groups of persons the system is intended to be used on). These characteristics can be satisfied by individual data sets or by a combination of data sets.

bench:qa:15.answer_text:
For a high‑risk AI system, the technical documentation must:

- Be drawn up in a way that demonstrates the system’s compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and provides national competent authorities and notified bodies with the necessary information, in a clear and comprehensive form, to assess that compliance.
- Contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV.

bench:qa:16.answer_text: Providers must keep the technical documentation for high-risk AI systems at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service.

bench:qa:17.answer_text:
Under Article 12, high-risk AI systems must have logging capabilities that:

- Enable recording of events relevant to: (a) identifying situations that may result in the system presenting a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) or in a substantial modification; (b) facilitating post-market monitoring; and (c) monitoring the operation of certain high-risk AI systems (those referred to in Article 26(5)).

In addition, for high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III, point 1(a), providers must ensure logging capabilities provide at least:
- The period of each use of the system (start date/time and end date/time).
- The reference database against which input data has been checked.
- The input data for which the search led to a match.
- The identification of the natural persons involved in verifying the results (as referred to in Article 14(5)).

bench:qa:18.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep the automatically generated logs (to the extent under their control) for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, and in any event for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (in particular Union law on personal data protection).

bench:qa:19.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems, deployers must be given (via the system’s instructions for use) information about the system’s characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations that is sufficient to enable deployers to interpret the system’s output and use it appropriately (where applicable). In addition, the provider must provide the system to the deployer in a way that enables the natural persons assigned to human oversight to remain aware of the risk of automatically relying or over‑relying on the system’s output (automation bias), as appropriate and proportionate (notably where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions by natural persons).

bench:qa:21.answer_text: Under Article 20, a provider must withdraw or recall a high‑risk AI system when it considers, or has reason to consider, that a high‑risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation. In that case, the provider must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, as appropriate, including bringing it into conformity or withdrawing/recalling it.

bench:qa:22.answer_text:
Upon a reasoned request by a competent authority, providers of high-risk AI systems must:

- Provide the authority with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate the system’s conformity with the Section 2 requirements, in a language easily understood by the authority and in an official EU language indicated by the Member State concerned.
- Also give the requesting authority access to the high-risk AI system’s automatically generated logs (as referred to in Article 12(1)), to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

In addition, the authority’s request for information must state its legal basis and purpose, specify the required information, set a deadline for providing it, and indicate the potential fines for supplying incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information.

bench:qa:23.answer_text:
A provider must appoint an authorised representative when the provider is established in a third country:

- For **high-risk AI systems**: the provider must, **by written mandate**, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union **prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market**.
- For **general-purpose AI models**: the provider must, **by written mandate**, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union **prior to placing the general-purpose AI model on the Union market**.

bench:qa:24.answer_text: Before placing a high‑risk AI system on the market, importers shall ensure the system is in conformity with the Regulation by verifying that: (a) the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure (Article 43); (b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV); (c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and instructions for use; and (d) the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1).

bench:qa:26.answer_text:
A distributor is considered a provider of a high‑risk AI system (and becomes subject to the provider obligations under Article 16) when any of these applies:

1) The distributor puts its name or trademark on a high‑risk AI system that has already been placed on the market or put into service (without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating obligations otherwise).

2) The distributor makes a substantial modification to a high‑risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, and the system remains high‑risk under Article 6.

3) The distributor modifies the intended purpose of an AI system (including a general‑purpose AI system) that was not classified as high‑risk and was already placed on the market or put into service, so that it becomes a high‑risk AI system in accordance with Article 6.

bench:qa:27.answer_text:
Main obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems (from the provided extracts) include:

- Use the system in accordance with the instructions for use by taking appropriate technical and organisational measures (including as referenced in Article 26(3) and (6)).
- Monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use.
- Keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent those logs are under the deployer’s control, for an appropriate period and in any event at least six months (unless Union or national law provides otherwise, notably data protection law).
- Public-authority deployers (and Union institutions/bodies/offices/agencies) must comply with the registration obligations in Article 49.
- Certain deployers (bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of certain Annex III point 5(b)/(c) systems) must, before deploying certain high-risk AI systems, perform a fundamental-rights impact assessment (with an exception for systems intended to be used in the area listed in Annex III point 2).
- For Annex III high-risk AI systems that make or assist decisions related to natural persons, inform the affected natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system (with a specific rule for law-enforcement use).

(Article 26 is explicitly identified as containing deployer obligations.)

bench:qa:28.answer_text:
Deployers must conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment **prior to deploying** a **high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2)** when they are:
- **bodies governed by public law**, or
- **private entities providing public services**, and
- **deployers of the high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III, points 5(b) and 5(c)**.

This obligation does **not** apply to **high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in Annex III, point 2** (exception).

If any of the Article 27 obligations are already met through a **data protection impact assessment (DPIA)** under GDPR Article 35 or Directive (EU) 2016/680 Article 27, the fundamental rights impact assessment must **complement** that DPIA.

bench:qa:29.answer_text: Under Article 28, the notifying authority’s role is to assess, designate, notify and monitor notified bodies. In doing so, it must be able to obtain and review relevant documentation from notified bodies to conduct those activities. It also has an information-sharing role vis-à-vis the Commission (providing, on request, all relevant information relating to the notification or the maintenance of a notified body’s competence). Where a notified body’s designation is restricted, suspended or withdrawn, the notifying authority must ensure the notified body’s files are kept and made available, on request, to notifying authorities in other Member States and to market surveillance authorities.

bench:qa:30.answer_text: When applying for notification, a conformity‑assessment body must submit an application to the notifying authority of the Member State where it is established. The application must be accompanied by: (1) a description of the conformity‑assessment activities, the conformity‑assessment module(s), and the types of AI systems for which it claims competence; (2) an accreditation certificate (if one exists) issued by a national accreditation body attesting it meets the Article 31 requirements; and (3) any valid document related to existing designations of the applicant under other Union harmonisation legislation.

bench:qa:31.answer_text:
The provided context does not include the text of Article 31 itself, so it does not specify the concrete requirements (e.g., independence, competence, resources, etc.) that Article 31 imposes on notified bodies.

From the provisions you provided, we can only infer the following about Article 31 requirements:
- A notifying authority may notify only conformity assessment bodies that have satisfied the requirements laid down in Article 31. 
- Notified bodies designated under other Union harmonisation legislation must keep their designation documentation updated when relevant changes occur so the authority responsible for notified bodies can monitor and verify continuous compliance with all Article 31 requirements.
- Certain notified bodies notified under other legal acts may control conformity of high-risk AI systems under the AI Act only if their compliance with specific Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) requirements has been assessed in the notification procedure under those legal acts.
- Third-country conformity assessment bodies may be authorised to carry out notified-body activities under the AI Act if they meet Article 31 requirements or ensure an equivalent level of compliance.

To list the actual “requirements for notified bodies under Article 31,” the text of Article 31 would be needed; it is not included in the supplied excerpts.

bench:qa:32.answer_text:
A provider can use a European harmonised standard to demonstrate conformity (i.e., benefit from a presumption of conformity) once the harmonised standard’s reference has been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, and only to the extent that the standard covers the relevant requirements/obligations.

For high-risk AI systems, if harmonised standards do not exist/are not available, are only partly applied, are not applied, or are published with a restriction (for the restricted part), the provider must instead follow the Annex VII conformity assessment procedure to demonstrate compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

For providers of general-purpose AI models (including those with systemic risk), compliance with European harmonised standards grants a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the applicable obligations; until a harmonised standard is published, they may rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance.

bench:qa:33.answer_text:
“Common specifications” are Commission-developed technical specifications intended to support the Regulation (alongside harmonised standards). When a high-risk AI system or a general-purpose AI model is in conformity with the relevant common specifications (or parts of them), it is presumed to be in conformity with the corresponding requirements/obligations to the extent those common specifications cover them.

They are used particularly as a reference point for conformity/compliance (presumption of conformity), and they may be relevant in situations where harmonised standards do not exist and common specifications are not available (e.g., as a condition referenced in conformity assessment-related provisions). When drafting common specifications, the Commission must consult the advisory forum.

Separately, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for implementing certain obligations if it deems a code is not adequate (this is not itself a “common specification”, but it is another form of Commission specification used to operationalise obligations).

bench:qa:34.answer_text: From the provided excerpts, Article 42 “presumption of conformity” relates to harmonised standards or common specifications that confer a presumption that an AI system complies with the Regulation’s requirements. This is reflected in the Act’s reference to “shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications … conferring a presumption of conformity.”

bench:qa:35.answer_text:
High-risk AI systems listed in Annex III must undergo the relevant conformity-assessment procedure “as referred to in Article 43”. Providers must ensure this procedure is carried out before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and importers must verify that the provider has carried it out before placing the system on the market.
